Ansible.explanation: The Ansible provisioner runs an Ansible playbook during a Packer build. Packer creates a temporary inventory, starts an SSH server, invokes ansible-playbook, and sends the play to the machine being built. It can also install roles or collections before the playbook runs.

interview.question: What does the Ansible provisioner do?
interview.answer: The provisioner runs an Ansible playbook during image creation. It creates an inventory for the target, starts an SSH server, runs ansible-playbook, and forwards the playbook through that server.
interview.followUp: How can you debug an Ansible failure? Add -vvvv to extra_arguments to enable verbose Ansible logging.

interview.question: Which settings are needed to run a playbook?
interview.answer: playbook_file is required and identifies the playbook to run. The command option can change the executable, but it defaults to ansible-playbook.
interview.followUp: What limitation applies to command? It must be a path to an executable, so shell scripting belongs in a separate executable script.

interview.question: How does inventory handling work?
interview.answer: Packer normally creates a temporary inventory and removes it after provisioning. You can provide inventory_file, or keep the generated file with keep_inventory_file for debugging.
interview.followUp: When is keep_inventory_file ignored? It has no effect when inventory_file is set.

keyPoints: Use this provisioner to apply an Ansible playbook while Packer builds an image.
By default, Packer creates an SSH-based inventory for the machine under construction.
playbook_file is required. It points to the playbook that Ansible will execute.
Packer can generate temporary SSH keys for the connection between Ansible and the target.
Set keep_inventory_file to true when you need the generated inventory for troubleshooting.
Add -vvvv to extra_arguments to get detailed Ansible logs.
gotchas: A remote_user setting in an Ansible task does not control the connection. Set the provisioner's user instead.
Extra arguments are passed directly. Do not write them as shell commands or add shell-style quoting.
The command option must name an executable. A string containing arbitrary shell script will not work.

Argo CD.summary: Kubernetes is an open source system for automating the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. It offers concepts, tutorials, cluster setup guidance, and task-oriented instructions.
Argo CD.explanation: Kubernetes provides an API and a set of components for running containerized applications. You declare the desired state, such as the number of application replicas, and Kubernetes works to make the cluster match that state. Tools such as kubectl send commands to the Kubernetes API.

kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=3
kubectl get pods
example.explanation: This creates a deployment, changes its desired replica count, and lists the resulting Pods.

interview.question: What is Kubernetes?
interview.answer: Kubernetes is an open source system for orchestrating containers. It automates application deployment, scaling, and management.
interview.followUp: What does scaling mean here? It means changing the desired number of running application instances so Kubernetes can maintain that state.

interview.question: How do users interact with Kubernetes?
interview.answer: A Kubernetes cluster is made from components that provide the control plane and run workloads. Kubernetes exposes an API, and users commonly interact with it through kubectl.
interview.followUp: Why use an API? The API gives tools and other systems a consistent way to inspect and change cluster state.

interview.question: How can someone start using Kubernetes?
interview.answer: Kubernetes supports different ways to learn and run clusters, including local tutorials, learning environments, and production environments. Cluster setup depends on your resources and needs.
interview.followUp: Which setup should a team choose? A production environment is appropriate for real services, while a learning environment is useful for practice and experiments.

gotchas: Kubernetes manages containers, but it is not itself a container image or container runtime.

interview.followUp: How could teams manage these deployments consistently across environments? A GitOps workflow can store the Helm configuration and apply changes through a version-controlled process.

Blue-Green Deployment.sourceTitle: Zero-downtime Deployment in Kubernetes with Jenkins
Blue-Green Deployment.summary: A blue-green deployment runs separate blue and green environments. Test the new environment, then switch the production service to it so users move to the new version.
Blue-Green Deployment.explanation: A blue-green deployment keeps two similar environments. Test the new environment through its test service, then change the production service to send users to it. The page also describes a Jenkins pipeline with an optional approval step before switching traffic.
Blue-Green Deployment.syntax: Deployment strategy with two environments and a production Service selector switch

example.title: Rolling update Deployment
example.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1
      maxSurge: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:1.27
example.explanation: This Deployment replaces pods gradually while keeping the service available.

useCases.title: Low-interruption releases
useCases.scenario: Release a new application version while keeping the current version available.

useCases.title: Pre-production validation
useCases.scenario: Test a new environment before exposing it to users.

useCases.title: Automated traffic switching
useCases.scenario: Move production traffic to a prepared version through a Jenkins pipeline.

interview.question: What is a blue-green deployment?
interview.answer: A blue-green deployment uses two similar environments. One serves production traffic, while the other receives the new version and can be tested before traffic is switched.
interview.followUp: How is traffic switched? The production service is changed from the current environment to the tested environment.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the test services?
interview.answer: The test services are connected to their matching deployments. They let you check whether the new environment is ready before changing the production service.
interview.followUp: Why keep separate test services? They allow validation without exposing the new environment to all users.

interview.question: How can Jenkins require approval before switching?
interview.answer: The Jenkins pipeline can add a stage before the switch. It can send an email and pause for a user to confirm that the deployment should continue.
interview.followUp: What must be configured for email approval? Jenkins needs SMTP server details in its system configuration.

keyPoints: Keep two deployments for the blue and green environments. They hold the old and new application versions separately.
Use one test service for each environment. Test the new version through its service before production traffic changes.
Use one production service as the public entry point. It initially sends traffic to the blue environment.
Start with production traffic on blue. Switch the production service to green only after green passes validation.
A Jenkins pipeline can automate the blue-green process on Kubernetes, including deployment and traffic switching.
gotchas: The sample template does not include email approval by default. Add SMTP settings and a confirmation stage if approval is required.

Canary Deployment.sourceTitle: Deploy a Release Using a Canary Deployment
Canary Deployment.summary: A canary deployment runs a new application version beside the stable version. A Service sends traffic to both, while monitoring and replica changes support a gradual rollout or quick rollback.
Canary Deployment.explanation: A canary deployment runs a new application version beside the stable version. A Service selects labels shared by both Deployments, so traffic reaches both versions. Replica counts influence the traffic share; monitoring results guide scaling, rollout, or rollback.
Canary Deployment.syntax:
kubectl apply -f <manifest>
kubectl scale deployment/<name> --replicas=<count>
kubectl rollout status deployment/<name>

example.title: Run a canary rollout
example.code:
kubectl apply -f https://k8s.io/examples/application/canary/app-v2-deployment.yaml
kubectl get deployments -l app.kubernetes.io/name=rollout-demo
kubectl get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=rollout-demo
kubectl logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=rollout-demo,track=canary --tail=50
kubectl scale deployment/rollout-demo-canary --replicas=2
kubectl rollout status deployment/rollout-demo-stable
example.explanation: This applies a canary Deployment, checks both releases, reviews canary logs, increases canary capacity, and waits for the stable Deployment rollout.

useCases.title: Risk-controlled release testing
useCases.scenario: Test a new application version with a small amount of live traffic before full release.

useCases.title: Gradual traffic increase
useCases.scenario: Increase the new version's replica count after monitoring shows acceptable behavior.

useCases.title: Fast rollback and diagnosis

interview.question: How does a Kubernetes canary deployment work?
interview.answer: Create two Deployments with different names and track labels, such as stable and canary. Give them a shared application label and use a Service selector that omits track, so the Service sends traffic to both.
interview.followUp: How can exact traffic percentages be set? Use separate Services and an HTTPRoute with backend weights, such as 90 for stable and 10 for canary.

interview.question: How do you increase traffic to a canary?
interview.answer: Start the canary with fewer replicas than the stable release. Observe logs, Pod status, and resource use, then increase canary replicas when it behaves correctly.
interview.followUp: What limits replica-based traffic control? The ratio is approximate because traffic is distributed across available endpoints; HTTPRoute weights provide explicit percentages.

interview.question: How do you roll back a canary?
interview.answer: Scale the canary to zero so it stops receiving traffic while its Deployment remains available for inspection. Restore stable capacity if needed, investigate, and delete the canary after the review.
interview.followUp: How is a successful rollout consolidated? Update the stable Deployment image and version configuration, wait for rollout status to complete, then delete the canary Deployment.

keyPoints: Run the new release beside the existing release instead of replacing it immediately.
Use a track label to distinguish stable Pods from canary Pods.
A Service can select labels shared by both releases, allowing traffic to reach both.
Changing replica counts changes the approximate share of traffic received by each release.
Review the canary during the test for failures, slow behavior, and unexpected results.
A problem can be handled by scaling the canary down and restoring stable capacity.
gotchas: A Deployment Pod template must use restartPolicy Always, which is also the default.
kubectl top cannot show resource use unless metrics-server is installed.
Manage the Deployment rather than editing its owned ReplicaSets directly.

CircleCI.sourceTitle: Secure CircleCI secrets with HashiCorp Vault | Well-Architected Framework | HashiCorp Developer
CircleCI.summary: Use CircleCI's organization-scoped OIDC token to log in to Vault without storing a long-lived secret. Bind the Vault role to claims such as project, context, and branch, then read only the required secrets.
CircleCI.explanation: CircleCI gives a job an organization-specific OIDC token. The job sends the v2 token to Vault's JWT login endpoint. Vault checks the issuer, signature, audience, and bound claims, then returns a short-lived token with only the role's policies. The job uses that token to read the required secrets.

parameters.name: jwt
parameters.description: The CircleCI OIDC token issued to the job.

parameters.name: role
parameters.description: The Vault JWT role selected for the job.

parameters.name: bound_claims
parameters.description: Claims that must match before Vault accepts the token.

parameters.name: token_policies
parameters.description: Policies attached to the issued Vault token.

parameters.name: ttl
parameters.description: Lifetime of the issued Vault token.

CircleCI.returns: A short-lived Vault token. The token can read only paths allowed by the policies attached to the matching role.

example.title: Authenticate a CircleCI job with Vault
example.code:
vault write auth/jwt/config \
  oidc_discovery_url="https://oidc.circleci.com/org/your-org-id"

vault write auth/jwt/role/circleci-production-deploy \
  role_type=jwt \
  user_claim=sub \
  bound_audiences="your-org-id" \
  bound_claims='{ "oidc.circleci.com/project-id": "your-project-id", "oidc.circleci.com/context-ids": ["your-context-id"], "oidc.circleci.com/vcs-ref": "refs/heads/main" }' \
  token_policies=circleci-production-deploy-policy \
  ttl=15m

VAULT_TOKEN=$(vault write -field=token auth/jwt/login \
  role=circleci-production-deploy \
  jwt=$CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN_V2)

export DATABASE_PASSWORD=$(vault kv get -field=password secret/ci/production/db)
example.explanation: Configure Vault to trust the CircleCI organization's OIDC issuer, bind a role to a project, context, and branch, then exchange the job token for a short-lived Vault token.

interview.question: How does a CircleCI job authenticate to Vault?
interview.answer: CircleCI issues an OIDC token to the job. The job sends it to Vault's JWT login endpoint. Vault validates it and returns a short-lived token whose policies control secret access.
interview.followUp: How can access be limited to one deployment path? Bind the Vault role to the project ID, context ID, and a main-branch VCS reference.

interview.question: Which CircleCI claims should a Vault role check?
interview.answer: The issuer setting must use the OIDC discovery URL for the specific CircleCI organization. Vault roles can then check claims such as project ID, context membership, and VCS reference.
interview.followUp: Why is a shared issuer unsafe here? It could allow tokens from other organizations to be trusted by the same configuration.

interview.question: When should a self-hosted runner use another Vault auth method?
interview.answer: JWT/OIDC is suitable for CircleCI cloud executors because CircleCI supplies the workload identity. Self-hosted runners can instead use AWS, Azure, GCP, or Kubernetes identity when their infrastructure provides it.
interview.followUp: What is the fallback for air-gapped CircleCI Server? Use AppRole with response wrapping, or TLS certificate authentication for persistent runner fleets.

keyPoints: A job can prove its identity to Vault without storing a long-lived Vault credential in CircleCI.
Vault can restrict access by project, context, branch, or tag.
A context claim adds an administrator-controlled approval boundary to project-based access.
Keep the Vault token short-lived and request only the secret values needed by the job.
JWT/OIDC is available for cloud executors and self-hosted runners that can reach CircleCI's OIDC endpoint.
A self-hosted runner can authenticate through its cloud platform identity instead of a bootstrap secret.
gotchas: Use the issuer URL for the exact CircleCI organization. Configure separate JWT auth settings when several organizations use the same Vault.
Do not create a role that accepts every token from the organization. Bind it at least to the project, and also to a context when possible.
Use CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN_V2 for new workflows instead of the older token variable.

CloudFormation.sourceTitle: Terraform versus CloudFormation, Heat, and other infrastructure as code tools
CloudFormation.summary: Terraform uses configuration files to define infrastructure and can combine multiple providers in one configuration. Its execution plan lets operators review resource changes before applying them.
CloudFormation.explanation: Terraform uses configuration files to define infrastructure, but it can combine resources from different providers in one configuration. It also creates an execution plan before applying changes, so you can review which resources Terraform will create, change, or destroy.

example.title: Run a CloudFormation template with Terraform

useCases.scenario: A team manages infrastructure across AWS, OpenStack, and external services.

interview.question: What is a main difference between Terraform and CloudFormation?
interview.answer: Terraform can manage resources from multiple providers in one configuration. For example, it can coordinate AWS and OpenStack resources and also use services such as Cloudflare or DNSimple.
interview.followUp: How can a team review changes before applying them? Run terraform plan, inspect the proposed actions, and then limit execution to that plan.

interview.question: What does terraform plan do?
interview.answer: terraform plan refreshes the current state and compares it with the configuration. It produces an action plan showing resources to create, modify, or destroy, which operators can inspect before execution.
interview.followUp: How can dependencies be examined? Use terraform graph to visualize the plan and its dependent ordering.

interview.question: How can existing CloudFormation resources be moved to Terraform?
interview.answer: Terraform keeps state information about managed resources and compares that state with the configuration. During migration, existing resources can be imported so Terraform can manage them without recreating them.
interview.followUp: What is another migration option? Terraform can temporarily run an existing CloudFormation template through the aws_cloudformation_stack resource.

keyPoints: Terraform defines infrastructure in configuration files and is not limited to one cloud platform.
One configuration can combine resources and services from several providers.
A single Terraform configuration can coordinate AWS and OpenStack infrastructure.
Terraform gives operators one syntax instead of separate tools for each platform or service.
The execution plan lists resources that Terraform will create, remove, or change.
terraform graph helps show the order created by resource dependencies.
gotchas: Moving a CloudFormation template to Terraform is not an automatic one-to-one conversion. Check each resource and property manually.
CloudFormation targets AWS, while Terraform can manage resources from multiple providers. Their configuration languages and models differ.
Migrate in stages instead of changing everything at once. This lowers risk and makes troubleshooting and rollback easier.

ConfigMap.summary: A ConfigMap stores non-confidential configuration as key-value pairs. Pods can use its values as environment variables, command arguments, or files in a volume.
ConfigMap.explanation: A ConfigMap stores non-confidential settings as key-value pairs. A Pod can use those values as environment variables, command arguments, or files in a volume, which keeps configuration separate from the container image.
ConfigMap.syntax:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: <name>
data: {}
# Optional: binaryData, immutable

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: Configuration values stored as UTF-8 strings. Keys may contain letters, digits, hyphens, underscores, or periods.

parameters.name: binaryData
parameters.description: Binary values represented as base64-encoded strings. Keys must not overlap with data keys.

parameters.name: immutable
parameters.description: When true, prevents changes to data and binaryData after creation.

parameters.name: metadata.name
parameters.description: The ConfigMap name. It must be a valid DNS subdomain name.

example.title: Use a ConfigMap in a Pod
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-settings
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: config-demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:latest
      command: ["sh", "-c", "echo $LOG_LEVEL; sleep 3600"]
      envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: app-settings
example.explanation: This creates a ConfigMap and makes all its data keys available as container environment variables.

useCases.scenario: Set different values for local, test, and production deployments without rebuilding the image.

interview.question: What is a ConfigMap used for?
interview.answer: A ConfigMap stores non-secret configuration in key-value pairs. Pods can consume it through environment variables, command arguments, mounted files, or direct Kubernetes API access.
interview.followUp: How can an application observe updates?

interview.question: How can a Pod consume ConfigMap data as environment variables?
interview.answer: Use envFrom with configMapRef to expose all keys, or use env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef to select one key. The selected key can have a different environment variable name.
interview.followUp: What happens if a key is not valid for a Pod environment variable?

interview.question: What does an immutable ConfigMap do?
interview.answer: Set immutable to true when creating the ConfigMap. Its data and binaryData cannot then be changed; only metadata can be modified.
interview.followUp: How do you change an immutable ConfigMap?

keyPoints: Use ConfigMaps for settings that are not secret.
A Pod has several ways to read ConfigMap values.
A normal Pod reference must point to a ConfigMap in the same namespace.
Put text values in data.
Use binaryData for bytes that are not valid UTF-8.
The immutable option was introduced in Kubernetes v1.19.
gotchas: Do not store passwords or other confidential data in a ConfigMap. Use a Secret instead.
A ConfigMap is not suitable for large configuration data.
Restart the Pod after changing a ConfigMap used through environment variables.
Do not use a subPath mount when the container must receive later updates.

Configuration Management.summary: Kubernetes separates application code from runtime configuration. ConfigMap and Secret objects store values that Pods or other components can load, while Secrets are for sensitive information.
Configuration Management.explanation: Kubernetes separates application code from configuration so the same container image can run in different environments. ConfigMap and Secret objects store configuration for Pods or other components to load; Secrets are intended for sensitive values.

example.title: Use a ConfigMap value in a Pod
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-settings
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: config-demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "echo $LOG_LEVEL; sleep 3600"]
      env:
        - name: LOG_LEVEL
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: app-settings
              key: LOG_LEVEL
example.explanation: This creates a ConfigMap and loads one value into a container environment variable.

useCases.scenario: Configure TLS-related cases using certificate-focused API kinds.

interview.question: Why separate configuration from a container image?
interview.answer: Kubernetes uses configuration objects to keep settings separate from application code. ConfigMap stores general configuration, while Secret is used for sensitive information such as passwords or tokens.
interview.followUp: When would a certificate-related API be relevant? CertificateSigningRequest and ClusterTrustBundle can hold configuration data for specific TLS-related cases.

interview.question: What is a ConfigMap used for?
interview.answer: A ConfigMap stores key-value configuration that a Pod or another component can load. This lets the same built image run with different settings in different contexts.
interview.followUp: What Kubernetes object is intended for sensitive values? Use a Secret rather than a ConfigMap for information such as passwords, OAuth tokens, or SSH keys.

interview.question: How does Kubernetes support secret management?
interview.answer: Kubernetes supports storing and managing sensitive information, including passwords, OAuth tokens, and SSH keys. Secrets and application configuration can be deployed or updated without rebuilding container images.
interview.followUp: Does Kubernetes automatically provide every application service? No. Kubernetes provides optional, pluggable building blocks and does not impose a single monolithic platform.

keyPoints: Kubernetes supports separating runtime configuration from application code.
The same application image can be used in tests and production with different configuration.
The two main configuration objects are ConfigMap and Secret.
A Pod or another component can load configuration stored in these objects.
Secret is intended for sensitive values such as passwords, OAuth tokens, and SSH keys.
Kubernetes lets operators deploy and update secrets and application configuration separately from image builds.
gotchas: Configuration and secrets can be updated without rebuilding the image, but sensitive data still needs careful handling.
ConfigMap and Secret are not the only configuration-related API kinds; some certificate APIs also hold configuration data.

Consul.sourceTitle: Consul on Kubernetes | Consul | HashiCorp Developer
Consul.summary: Consul integrates with Kubernetes through the Helm chart, Consul K8s CLI, service sync, and Consul Service Mesh. It can secure pod traffic with mutual TLS and connect Kubernetes services with services registered in Consul.
Consul.explanation: Consul runs on Kubernetes through official integrations such as the Helm chart, service synchronization, and Consul Service Mesh. In the mesh, Consul can inject a sidecar into pods so services use encrypted, authorized connections with mutual TLS. Kubernetes services can also be synchronized with the Consul service registry.

example.title: Install Consul with Helm
example.code:
helm repo add hashicorp https://helm.releases.hashicorp.com
helm repo update
helm install consul hashicorp/consul --set global.name=consul
example.explanation: This adds the HashiCorp Helm repository, updates its local index, and installs Consul with the default release name.

useCases.scenario: Run Consul Service Mesh for Kubernetes workloads.

useCases.title: Discover external services
useCases.scenario: Let Kubernetes workloads find services registered outside Kubernetes.

useCases.scenario: Let external workloads find services running in Kubernetes.

useCases.title: Operate Consul on Kubernetes
useCases.scenario: Deploy Consul on a Kubernetes cluster and use Kubernetes tools with it.

interview.question: How are Consul servers deployed on Kubernetes?
interview.answer: Consul servers run as a StatefulSet. Persistent volume claims preserve server state, including node identity, when a pod moves to a new IP address. Anti-affinity spreads servers across different Kubernetes nodes.
interview.followUp: How does a server know when it is ready? Its readiness probe reports ready only after the server has established a leader.

interview.question: How does Consul Service Mesh secure pod traffic?
interview.answer: Consul can inject a sidecar into application pods. The sidecar enables encrypted and authorized connections with mutual TLS between services, including communication with external services.
interview.followUp: What changes in the newer Kubernetes deployment model? Consul dataplane manages Envoy proxies without requiring client agents on every node.

interview.question: What problem does service synchronization solve?
interview.answer: Service sync copies Kubernetes services into the Consul service registry. Kubernetes workloads can discover external Consul services through Kubernetes discovery, while external workloads can discover Kubernetes services through Consul.
interview.followUp: What is another way to install Consul? The documentation describes installing it with the official Helm chart or the Consul K8s CLI.

keyPoints: The documented installation choices include the Helm chart and the Consul K8s CLI.
The service mesh can add a sidecar to application pods automatically.
The injected sidecar supports encrypted, authorized traffic between services by using mutual TLS.
Service sync connects Kubernetes service discovery with the Consul registry.
Consul server agents use a StatefulSet and persistent volume claims to keep server state.
Consul servers join the cluster through the Kubernetes Service DNS name.
gotchas: Do not upgrade to a Kubernetes version marked with an asterisk until its testing is complete.
Deleting the StatefulSet does not remove persistent volumes or claims automatically; remove them yourself when needed.

container registry.sourceTitle: Pull an Image from a Private Registry
container registry.summary: Use a Kubernetes Secret to authenticate a Pod to a private container registry. Create the Secret from Docker credentials and reference it with imagePullSecrets.
container registry.explanation: Kubernetes can pull a private image by using a Secret with registry credentials. Create a Secret from an existing Docker configuration, then list that Secret in the Pod's imagePullSecrets field. The Secret must use the kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson type, and the credential data must use the .dockerconfigjson key.

parameters.name: imagePullSecrets
parameters.description: The Secret name used by the Pod for registry credentials.

parameters.name: image
parameters.description: The private image reference to pull.

example.title: Pull an image from a private registry
example.code:
kubectl create secret generic regcred \
  --from-file=.dockerconfigjson=$HOME/.docker/config.json \
  --type=kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson

cat <<'EOF' > pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: private-image-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: private.example/app:1.0
  imagePullSecrets:
    - name: regcred
EOF
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
example.explanation: This creates a registry credential Secret and tells the Pod to use it when pulling the private image.

useCases.title: Pull a private application image
useCases.scenario: A Pod needs an image stored in a private registry.

useCases.title: Reuse Docker login credentials
useCases.scenario: A team already authenticated with Docker on a workstation.

useCases.title: Share node-level registry access
useCases.scenario: Several Pods need access to a registry.

interview.question: How does a Pod pull an image from a private registry?
interview.answer: Create a Secret of type kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson from registry credentials. Reference its name in the Pod's imagePullSecrets field so kubelet can use it while pulling the image.
interview.followUp: How can a cluster provide registry access without adding the Secret to every Pod? Configure nodes to authenticate to the private registry, or use a kubelet credential provider plugin.

interview.question: What format must the registry Secret use?
interview.answer: The Secret must contain the Docker configuration under the .dockerconfigjson data key. Its type must be kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson.
interview.followUp: What changes if the Docker client uses a credentials store? The configuration may contain credsStore instead of an auth entry, so create the Kubernetes Secret directly as described by the documentation.

interview.question: How are container image names resolved?
interview.answer: A registry hostname can include a port, and the image name can include that hostname. If no registry hostname is given, Kubernetes assumes the Docker public registry unless the runtime has a different default configured.
interview.followUp: How should restricted environments handle Kubernetes release images? Mirror them to a private registry that the environment controls, because registry.k8s.io can redirect pulls to changing backend locations.

keyPoints: Use a Secret with type kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson for registry authentication.
Add the credential Secret name to the Pod's imagePullSecrets field.
An existing Docker login configuration can be imported into a Kubernetes Secret.
When writing the Secret manually, store the encoded Docker configuration under .dockerconfigjson.
Private registries may require authentication both to find an image and to pull it.
Node-level registry authentication can make the configured private registries available to all Pods.
gotchas: A Pod must reference the credential Secret with imagePullSecrets. Otherwise, it cannot use that private registry credential.
Use a separate registry Secret for each registry when a Pod needs credentials for more than one registry.
Do not depend on the old built-in cloud registry credential providers in Kubernetes 1.26 or newer.

containerd.sourceTitle: containerd image store with Docker Engine
containerd.summary: The containerd image store is Docker's backend for pulling, pushing, and storing images. It uses snapshotters and supports multi-platform images, attestations, Wasm containers, and advanced image distribution features.
containerd.explanation: The containerd image store is Docker's backend for pulling, pushing, and keeping images. It uses snapshotters instead of classic drivers, so Docker can handle image indexes, attestations, Wasm containers, and alternative layer-storage methods.

example.title: Build a multi-platform image
example.code:
docker build --platform=linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t example/app:latest .
docker image inspect example/app:latest
example.explanation: Builds one image for two platforms and checks the image in the local store.

useCases.title: Multi-platform development
useCases.scenario: Build and test one image for amd64 and arm64 on a local machine.

useCases.title: Supply-chain attestations
useCases.scenario: Keep provenance or SBOM data with an image.

useCases.title: Lazy pulling
useCases.scenario: Start containers before every image layer is downloaded.

useCases.title: Wasm containers
useCases.scenario: Run WebAssembly workloads through Docker.

interview.question: What is the containerd image store?
interview.answer: It is Docker's image storage backend. It manages image pulling, pushing, and local storage through containerd snapshotters.
interview.followUp: What does it enable that classic storage does not? It supports local multi-platform images, attestations, Wasm containers, and pluggable snapshotters.

interview.question: When is it enabled by default?
interview.answer: Docker Engine 29.0 and later use it by default on fresh installations. Older upgraded installations must enable the containerd-snapshotter feature in daemon.json.
interview.followUp: How can you verify it? Run docker info -f '{{ .DriverStatus }}' and look for io.containerd.snapshotter.v1.

interview.question: How do you enable it on Docker Engine?
interview.answer: Add containerd-snapshotter=true under features in /etc/docker/daemon.json, restart Docker, and verify the driver status. Existing overlay2 data stays on disk but becomes hidden.
interview.followUp: How do you preserve old images? Push them to a registry or export them with docker save before switching.

keyPoints: Containerd stores image and container data with snapshotters rather than drivers such as overlay2.
You can build and keep images for several CPU platforms in the local store.
The store supports image attestations, including provenance and software bills of materials.
It supports containers that use WebAssembly workloads.
Alternative snapshotters can provide lazy image pulls or peer-to-peer distribution.
After enabling the store, overlayfs is the default containerd snapshotter.
gotchas: Changing stores does not delete the other store's data, but its images and containers are hidden until you switch back.
The store can use more disk space because it keeps compressed image data and extracted layers.
Do not enable this store with user namespace remapping.
With lazy pulling, a running image may still lack data needed for saving or pushing.

Continuous Delivery.summary: Kubernetes is an open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services. It uses declarative configuration and automation to help keep applications available.
Continuous Delivery.explanation: Kubernetes manages containerized workloads and services through declarative configuration and automation. It helps keep applications available by managing the containers that run them; for example, if one container stops, Kubernetes can start another.

example.title: Run and inspect a container
example.code:
kubectl run web --image=nginx --restart=Never
kubectl get pods
example.explanation: Creates one Pod from the nginx image, then lists Pods.

useCases.title: Manage containerized workloads
useCases.scenario: Run applications packaged as containers.

useCases.title: Support availability
useCases.scenario: Keep application containers running in production.

useCases.title: Use declarative operations
useCases.scenario: Describe desired application resources and let the platform manage them.

useCases.title: Build with the ecosystem
useCases.scenario: Use the surrounding tools and services available for Kubernetes.

interview.question: What is Kubernetes?
interview.answer: Kubernetes is a portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services. It supports declarative configuration and automation.
interview.followUp: What problem does it solve in production? It manages application containers and helps maintain availability when a container stops.

interview.question: Why do teams use Kubernetes for production workloads?
interview.answer: Containers package and run applications, but production systems must manage those containers and avoid downtime. Kubernetes provides a system that handles this management and can start another container when one goes down.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful beyond starting containers? The page presents container management and availability as core production needs.

interview.question: What does Kubernetes provide besides container execution?
interview.answer: Kubernetes uses declarative configuration and automation to manage containerized workloads and services. This gives teams a way to describe the desired setup and have the platform manage it.
interview.followUp: What ecosystem surrounds Kubernetes? The page says Kubernetes services, support, and tools are widely available.

keyPoints: Kubernetes is an open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services.
It supports declarative configuration and automation.
Production use requires managing the containers that run applications.
A production goal is to keep applications available without downtime.
Kubernetes can help replace a container when one stops.
The Kubernetes ecosystem includes widely available services, support, and tools.
gotchas: The production case study is old, so its details may no longer describe current Kubernetes practices.

Continuous Deployment.summary: A Deployment declares and manages desired updates for Pods and ReplicaSets. Its spec states the desired behavior, while status reports the latest observed state.
Continuous Deployment.explanation: A Deployment stores the desired behavior for Pods and ReplicaSets. Kubernetes compares that desired state with the observed state and updates the managed resources to move the cluster toward the desired result.
Continuous Deployment.syntax:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: ...
spec: ...

parameters.name: apiVersion
parameters.description: Versioned schema for the object.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: REST resource type represented by the object.

parameters.name: metadata
parameters.description: Standard metadata for the object.

parameters.name: spec
parameters.description: Desired behavior of the Deployment.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: Latest observed Deployment state.

Continuous Deployment.returns: A Deployment resource with desired behavior in spec and the latest observed state in status.

example.title: Create and inspect a Deployment
example.code:
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx
kubectl get deployment web
example.explanation: This creates a Deployment named web from the nginx image, then shows its current state.

useCases.title: Declarative application updates
useCases.scenario: You need Kubernetes to manage changes to a group of Pods through a declared target state.

useCases.title: Workload state management
useCases.scenario: You need one Kubernetes resource to describe desired Pod behavior and report its current state.

interview.question: What does a Deployment do?
interview.answer: A Deployment describes the desired behavior for Pods and ReplicaSets. It lets Kubernetes manage updates declaratively instead of requiring manual Pod changes.
interview.followUp: How would you find whether the desired state has been reached? Check the Deployment's status, which contains the most recently observed state.

interview.question: What are apiVersion and kind used for?
interview.answer: The apiVersion selects the versioned API schema for the object. For this resource, the documented value is apps/v1.
interview.followUp: What happens if the server does not recognize the version? It may reject the object rather than accepting an unknown schema.

interview.question: What is the difference between spec and status?
interview.answer: The spec contains the desired behavior of the Deployment. The status reports the latest state observed by Kubernetes.
interview.followUp: Why keep desired and observed state separate? This lets Kubernetes compare intent with reality and act to reconcile differences.

keyPoints: A Deployment provides declarative updates for Pods and ReplicaSets.
The spec field describes what the Deployment should do.
The status field records the latest state observed for the Deployment.
apiVersion identifies the versioned schema used by the object.
kind names the REST resource represented by the object.
gotchas: The API server can reject an unknown apiVersion, and recognized versions may be converted internally.
The kind field identifies the resource type and cannot be changed after creation.

Continuous Integration.summary: Kubernetes is an open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services. You declare the desired state, and Kubernetes continuously works to make the running state match it.
Continuous Integration.explanation: Kubernetes uses a declarative API and control processes. You state the desired state, such as the number of application replicas. Kubernetes continuously works to make the running state match that desired state. The platform is extensible, so different workloads and supporting tools can be used with it.

example.title: Create and scale a workload
example.code:
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx
kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=3
kubectl get pods
example.explanation: These commands create a Deployment, set three desired replicas, and show the resulting Pods.

useCases.scenario: Run applications packaged as containers across a cluster.

useCases.title: Maintain availability
useCases.scenario: Keep multiple copies of an application running.

useCases.title: Run varied workloads
useCases.scenario: Support different application types, from stateless services to stateful and data-processing workloads.

useCases.title: Assemble a platform
useCases.scenario: Build a developer platform while choosing separate tools for delivery, logging, monitoring, and application services.

interview.question: What is Kubernetes?
interview.answer: Kubernetes is a platform for managing containerized workloads and services. It supports declarative configuration and automation. It is designed to support stateless, stateful, and data-processing workloads.
interview.followUp: What happens when a container stops? Kubernetes can use its control processes to move the current state back toward the desired state, such as starting another container.

interview.question: How does Kubernetes manage workloads?
interview.answer: You describe the desired state through the Kubernetes API. Independent control processes continuously compare that target with the current state and act to reduce the difference.
interview.followUp: Why is this different from orchestration? Orchestration usually defines a fixed sequence such as A, then B, then C; Kubernetes does not require one central workflow.

interview.question: What does Kubernetes deliberately not provide?
interview.answer: Kubernetes provides core building blocks, but it does not include every application service. Databases, caches, message buses, logging systems, and configuration systems remain choices for the user.
interview.followUp: Can these services work with Kubernetes? Yes. They can run on Kubernetes or be accessed by applications through portable integration mechanisms.

keyPoints: Kubernetes manages containerized workloads and services on a portable and extensible platform.
Its API supports declarative configuration: describe the target state instead of listing every operation.
The platform is intended for many workload types, including stateless, stateful, and data-processing applications.
An application that can run in a container is generally a candidate for Kubernetes.
Independent control processes continuously move the cluster toward the desired state.
Kubernetes does not require one central controller for every action.
gotchas: Kubernetes does not build or deploy application source code. Use a separate build and delivery process.
Kubernetes does not require one logging, monitoring, or alerting product.
Kubernetes is not only a step-by-step workflow runner. Its control processes work continuously toward the desired state.

CRD.sourceTitle: Extend the Kubernetes API with CustomResourceDefinitions
CRD.summary: A CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) adds a new resource type to the Kubernetes API. Kubernetes serves and stores its objects, while the CRD defines their names, scope, versions, and schema.
CRD.explanation: A CustomResourceDefinition adds a new resource type to the Kubernetes API. Kubernetes serves and stores objects of that type, using the CRD's group, version, names, scope, and OpenAPI schema. A CRD can be used without writing another API server, and controllers can watch its objects and act on them.

parameters.name: spec.group
parameters.description: The API group used in the custom resource API path.

parameters.name: spec.versions
parameters.description: The supported API versions, including served, storage, and schema settings.

parameters.name: spec.scope
parameters.description: The resource scope: Namespaced or Cluster.

parameters.name: spec.names
parameters.description: The plural, singular, kind, and optional short names used by the resource.

parameters.name: spec.versions[*].schema.openAPIV3Schema
parameters.description: The OpenAPI v3 schema for custom resource data.

CRD.returns: A new Kubernetes API resource endpoint and custom resource type.

example.title: Create a namespaced CRD
example.code:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: crontabs.stable.example.com
spec:
  group: stable.example.com
  names:
    plural: crontabs
    singular: crontab
    kind: CronTab
    shortNames:
      - ct
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                cronSpec:
                  type: string
                image:
                  type: string
kubectl apply -f crd.yaml
kubectl apply -f crontab.yaml
kubectl get ct
example.explanation: This defines and uses a namespaced CronTab resource.

useCases.title: Add a simple Kubernetes resource
useCases.scenario: Create a small API object with a few structured fields and manage it with kubectl.

useCases.title: Build controller-driven automation
useCases.scenario: Let a controller watch custom objects and create or update related Kubernetes objects.

useCases.title: Follow Kubernetes API conventions
useCases.scenario: Use Kubernetes metadata, status, RBAC, watch, and client-library behavior for a new resource.

interview.question: What does a CRD provide?
interview.answer: A CRD declaratively defines a new API resource with its group, versions, names, scope, and schema. The Kubernetes API server then serves and stores instances of that resource.
interview.followUp: When would an aggregated API be better? It is better when you need custom storage, arbitrary validation or business logic, conversions, or other API behavior that CRDs do not provide.

interview.question: How does CRD scope work?
interview.answer: The CRD's scope is either Namespaced or Cluster. Namespaced custom objects belong to a namespace, while cluster-scoped objects do not; the CRD object itself is always non-namespaced.
interview.followUp: What happens when a namespace is deleted? Kubernetes deletes all namespaced custom objects in that namespace.

interview.question: How are custom resources validated and protected during deletion?
interview.answer: The schema is an OpenAPI v3 schema under each served version. With apiextensions.k8s.io/v1, a structural schema is required, and it validates custom objects during creation and updates.
interview.followUp: How can a controller delay deletion? It adds a domain-qualified finalizer; deletion waits until the controller removes that finalizer.

keyPoints: A CRD defines a new custom resource type.
CRDs add API types without requiring a separate API server.
Set spec.scope to Namespaced or Cluster.
The Kubernetes API server handles the endpoint and storage for CRD objects.
A v1 CRD must include a structural OpenAPI schema.
OpenAPI v3 validation checks custom resource fields and types.
kubectl accepts resource names without case sensitivity and supports configured singular, plural, and short names.
gotchas: Deleting a CRD also deletes every custom object stored under it. Recreating the CRD starts with no custom objects.
Create RBAC rules for the new resource. Existing roles usually do not grant access automatically.
Unknown fields are normally removed before storage. Preserve them only for selected subtrees with the documented schema option.

DaemonSet.summary: A DaemonSet keeps one copy of a Pod on every eligible node. It is commonly used for node-level services such as logging, monitoring, and networking.
DaemonSet.explanation: A DaemonSet controller keeps one copy of a Pod on every eligible node. It creates Pods when nodes match the selection rules and removes them when nodes no longer match.
DaemonSet.syntax:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels: <labels>
  template: <pod template>

parameters.name: apiVersion
parameters.description: Identifies the DaemonSet API group and version.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: Must be DaemonSet.

parameters.name: metadata
parameters.description: Object identity, including a valid DNS subdomain name as its name.

parameters.name: spec
parameters.description: DaemonSet configuration, including the selector, Pod template, scheduling rules, and update strategy.

DaemonSet.returns: A Kubernetes DaemonSet resource that maintains Pods on eligible nodes.

example.title: Basic DaemonSet
example.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: node-logger
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: node-logger
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: node-logger
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: logger
        image: busybox:1.37
        command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do date; sleep 30; done"]
example.explanation: This creates one continuously running Pod on every eligible node.

useCases.title: Node log collection
useCases.scenario: A logging agent must read local node logs.

useCases.title: Node monitoring
useCases.scenario: A monitoring agent must run close to each node.

useCases.title: Cluster node support
useCases.scenario: A networking or storage helper must exist on each eligible node.

interview.question: What problem does a DaemonSet solve?
interview.answer: A DaemonSet makes sure that a Pod runs on every node, or on every node selected by its node selector or affinity. New matching nodes receive Pods, and Pods are removed when nodes stop matching.
interview.followUp: How does this differ from a Deployment? A Deployment manages a chosen replica count for services, while a DaemonSet targets specific hosts and keeps a copy on each eligible host.

interview.question: What must be true about the DaemonSet selector?
interview.answer: The selector identifies the Pods managed by the DaemonSet. It must match the labels in .spec.template.metadata.labels, and Kubernetes rejects a manifest when they differ.
interview.followUp: Why is the selector immutable? Changing it could leave existing Pods unmanaged or cause confusing adoption behavior.

interview.question: How do DaemonSet update strategies work?
interview.answer: RollingUpdate is the default strategy. When the Pod template changes, old Pods are replaced automatically in a controlled way; OnDelete waits for an administrator to delete old Pods before creating replacements.
interview.followUp: Which settings control a rolling update? maxUnavailable limits unavailable Pods, while minReadySeconds requires new Pods to remain ready for a specified time; maxSurge controls extra Pods.

keyPoints: Use a DaemonSet when node-level work needs one Pod on every node or on a selected group of nodes.
The controller reacts to new nodes and schedules the DaemonSet Pod when the node is eligible.
A DaemonSet contains a Pod template. The template uses the Pod schema but does not include apiVersion or kind.
The selector and template labels must agree. Kubernetes rejects configurations that do not match.
DaemonSet Pods receive built-in tolerations, including support for unschedulable nodes and several node pressure conditions.
Use nodeSelector or node affinity to restrict the DaemonSet to eligible nodes.
Changing the Pod template can trigger an automatic rolling replacement when the update strategy is RollingUpdate.
gotchas: You cannot change the Pod selector after creating the DaemonSet. Create a new DaemonSet if the selector must change.
A rolling update controls replacement so that no node runs more than one DaemonSet Pod at a time.
A high-priority DaemonSet Pod can evict existing Pods when the node lacks resources. Set a suitable priority only when this behavior is intended.

Deployment.summary: A Deployment declares how many application Pods should run and which Pod template to use. Kubernetes creates ReplicaSets and updates Pods until they match that declaration.
Deployment.explanation: A Deployment stores the desired state for an application’s Pods and ReplicaSets. Its controller creates or changes ReplicaSets until the running Pods match that state. When the Pod template changes, Kubernetes creates a new ReplicaSet and replaces Pods using a controlled rollout.
Deployment.syntax:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  replicas: <number>
  selector:
    matchLabels: <labels>
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: <labels>
    spec:
      containers: [...]

parameters.name: spec.replicas
parameters.description: Number of desired Pods. Defaults to 1.

parameters.name: spec.selector
parameters.description: Label selector for the Pods managed by the Deployment. It must match the template labels.

parameters.name: spec.template
parameters.description: Template used to create the Pods.

parameters.name: spec.strategy
parameters.description: Deployment replacement strategy: Recreate or RollingUpdate.

parameters.name: spec.minReadySeconds
parameters.description: Minimum time a new Pod must remain ready before it is available. Defaults to 0 seconds.

parameters.name: spec.progressDeadlineSeconds
parameters.description: Maximum time allowed for the Deployment to make progress before it is considered failed. Defaults to 600 seconds.

Deployment.returns: A Deployment object with status describing observed, ready, available, updated, and unavailable Pods.

example.title: A basic Deployment
example.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.25
example.explanation: This declares three nginx Pods. The selector must match the template label.

useCases.scenario: Change a container image or other Pod template setting without replacing every Pod at once.

useCases.scenario: Temporarily stop a rollout while making several template changes.

interview.question: What does a Deployment do?
interview.answer: A Deployment describes the desired state for Pods and ReplicaSets. The Deployment controller creates or adjusts ReplicaSets and keeps changing them until the actual state matches the desired state.
interview.followUp: What happens if a node fails? The controller replaces the lost application instance, potentially on another node.

interview.question: What starts a Deployment rollout?
interview.answer: Changing .spec.template, such as changing a container image, starts a rollout. Kubernetes creates a new ReplicaSet, increases its replicas, and decreases the old ReplicaSet in a controlled way.
interview.followUp: Does changing the replica count start a rollout? No. Scaling changes the number of Pods but does not change the Pod template.

interview.question: How does a rolling update limit disruption?
interview.answer: RollingUpdate is the default strategy. By default, up to 25% of desired Pods can be unavailable and up to 25% extra Pods can be created during the update.
interview.followUp: How can an update be delayed before a Pod counts as available? Set minReadySeconds to require the Pod to stay ready for a specified time.

keyPoints: A Deployment is mainly for workloads that do not keep application state in the Pods.
You declare the target state. The controller works toward that target.
The replicas field sets the desired number of Pods. A ReplicaSet creates and maintains them.
A rollout starts when the Pod template changes, such as when its labels or container image changes.
Each rollout creates a revision, which lets you track changes and roll back to an earlier revision.
revisionHistoryLimit controls how many old ReplicaSets remain available for rollback.
gotchas: Do not directly change ReplicaSets that a Deployment owns. Change the Deployment instead.
The selector must match the labels in the Pod template. Avoid overlapping selectors with other controllers.
Do not edit the automatically added pod-template-hash label.

Docker.summary: The Kubernetes driver runs BuildKit builders in Kubernetes pods. Buildx can use replicas, persistent cache storage, selected nodes, rootless mode, and multiple architectures.
Docker.explanation: The Kubernetes driver connects Docker Buildx to BuildKit pods in a Kubernetes cluster. Buildx creates the Kubernetes resources, while the builder configuration stays on the local machine. You can choose the namespace, replica count, resource limits, storage, node placement, load balancing, rootless mode, and supported platforms.

parameters.description: BuildKit image used by the pods.

parameters.name: namespace
parameters.description: Kubernetes namespace for the builder.

parameters.name: default-load
parameters.description: Loads built images into the Docker Engine image store automatically.

parameters.name: replicas
parameters.description: Number of BuildKit replicas.

parameters.name: persistent-volume-claim.requests.storage
parameters.description: Persistent storage size for each replica's build cache.

parameters.name: loadbalance
parameters.description: Balances builds with `sticky` or `random` behavior.

parameters.name: qemu.install
parameters.description: Installs QEMU for non-native builds when set to true.

parameters.name: rootless
parameters.description: Runs pods without a privileged security context when set to true.

example.title: Create and use a Kubernetes builder
example.code:
docker buildx create --bootstrap --name=kube --driver=kubernetes --driver-opt=namespace=buildkit,replicas=4

docker buildx build --builder=kube --platform=linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t example/app --push .
example.explanation: This creates a Kubernetes Buildx builder with four replicas, then builds and pushes an image for two platforms.

useCases.title: Use cluster compute
useCases.scenario: A CI system needs more build capacity than the local machine can provide.

useCases.title: Build for multiple architectures

useCases.scenario: Keep BuildKit cache across pod restarts.

interview.question: What does the Kubernetes driver do?
interview.answer: The Kubernetes driver lets Buildx use BuildKit running in Kubernetes pods. Create it with `docker buildx create`, then select it with `--builder`.
interview.followUp: How would you spread builds across replicas? Set `replicas` and choose `loadbalance=random` for even distribution, or keep the default `sticky` mode to use local cache.

interview.question: How can BuildKit cache survive pod restarts?
interview.answer: Set `persistent-volume-claim.requests.storage` to give each BuildKit replica persistent cache storage. Buildx creates a StatefulSet instead of a Deployment in this mode.
interview.followUp: What happens with four replicas? Each replica receives its own persistent volume claim, so its cache stays local to that pod across restarts.

interview.question: How do you build for multiple native architectures?
interview.answer: For native multi-platform builds, create one Buildx node for each architecture and use `--append` to add more nodes. Assign each node with a Kubernetes architecture selector.
interview.followUp: What is the difference between a Buildx node and a Kubernetes node? One Buildx node can connect to multiple Kubernetes nodes that share the same architecture.

keyPoints: It connects local development or CI environments to BuildKit builders running in a Kubernetes cluster.
`loadbalance=random` spreads work across replicas, while the default `sticky` mode favors the same replica and its cache.
Persistent volume cache storage changes the Kubernetes resource from a Deployment to a StatefulSet.
Use node selectors and tolerations to control where BuildKit pods are scheduled.
The driver supports multi-platform builds with QEMU or with native architectures in cluster nodes.
gotchas: QEMU can build for another architecture, but it can be much slower. Native nodes are better for compute-heavy work.
Quote CSV-style values such as node selectors and tolerations with single quotes in shell commands.
Rootless mode needs Kubernetes 1.19 or newer. Ubuntu is the recommended host kernel.

docker build.summary: Docker Build uses Buildx as the client and BuildKit as the backend. Buildx sends build requests to a builder, which executes the steps and produces an image or other artifacts.
docker build.explanation: The `docker build` command uses Buildx as its client. Buildx sends the build request to BuildKit, which solves the Dockerfile steps and creates an image or another build result. Builders can use different drivers and can run locally or connect to remote BuildKit daemons.

parameters.description: Optional builder name used for the build.

parameters.name: PATH | URL | -
parameters.description: Build context, such as the current directory.

docker build.returns: A container image or other build artifacts; the result may be returned to the client or uploaded to a registry.

example.title: Build with a chosen builder
example.code: docker buildx build --builder my_builder .
example.explanation: Builds the current directory with the named builder.

useCases.title: Create an image
useCases.scenario: Build a container image from a Dockerfile.

useCases.title: Run builds with custom builders
useCases.scenario: Use a separate or remote BuildKit setup.

useCases.title: Publish build results
useCases.scenario: Send build output to a container registry.

useCases.title: Inspect and switch builders
useCases.scenario: Manage several builder instances.

interview.question: What are Buildx and BuildKit?
interview.answer: Buildx is the client and BuildKit is the builder that executes the work. Buildx sends the request, and BuildKit resolves and runs the build steps.
interview.followUp: How can one client use different builders? Buildx decouples the client from BuildKit, so it can use local or remote builders.

interview.question: What is a builder?
interview.answer: A builder is a BuildKit daemon used to run builds. It solves Dockerfile steps and produces a container image or other artifacts.
interview.followUp: How can builders differ? Buildx supports drivers such as `docker`, `docker-container`, and `remote`, which select different BuildKit setups.

interview.question: How do you inspect and select builders?
interview.answer: `docker buildx ls` lists builder instances and marks the selected one with `*`. Use `docker buildx use <name>` to select another builder.
interview.followUp: How can `docker build` use a non-default builder? Add `--builder <name>` or set `BUILDX_BUILDER` for the command.

keyPoints: Buildx is the command-line client for starting and managing Docker builds.
BuildKit is the backend that executes the requested build.
A build can return its result to the client or send it to a registry.
The Docker CLI can create, inspect, manage, and connect to builders, including remote ones.
The default Docker Engine builder uses the `docker` driver.
Run `docker buildx ls` to list available builder instances.
gotchas: `docker build` does not automatically use a custom selected builder. Pass `--builder` or set `BUILDX_BUILDER` when needed.
Changing the Docker context also changes which daemon the default builder uses.

Docker Compose.summary: Docker Compose defines and runs multi-container applications from one YAML file. It manages services, networks, and volumes and provides commands for the application lifecycle.
Docker Compose.explanation: Compose reads a YAML file that describes the containers, networks, volumes, and settings for an application. The `docker compose up` command creates or updates the resources and starts the services; Compose can later stop, rebuild, inspect, or remove the application.

example.title: A small Compose application
example.code:
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
  db:
    image: mysql
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/mysql

volumes:
  db-data:
example.explanation: This file defines an app service built from a Dockerfile and a MySQL service. It maps port 3000 and keeps database files in a named volume.

useCases.scenario: Local development

useCases.title: Create the same service setup for test runs
useCases.scenario: Testing

useCases.scenario: CI workflows

useCases.scenario: Operations

interview.question: What problem does Docker Compose solve?
interview.answer: Compose lets you describe a multi-container application in one YAML file. It manages services and their related networks and volumes, then starts them together with a command.
interview.followUp: How does Compose handle a changed file? Run `docker compose up` again. Compose compares the declared setup with the current resources and applies the needed changes.

interview.question: What is the difference between a Dockerfile and a Compose file?
interview.answer: A Compose file defines running containers and their configuration. A Dockerfile contains image-build instructions; a Compose service can refer to that Dockerfile when it needs to build an image.
interview.followUp: Why use separate containers? The documentation recommends that each container do one thing well, such as running the application or the database.

interview.question: What happens when a Compose application is torn down?
interview.answer: `docker compose down` removes the application containers and its network. Named volumes remain by default so stored data can be used again when the stack starts.
interview.followUp: How can all stack data be removed? Add `--volumes` to the command: `docker compose down --volumes`.

keyPoints: Compose describes and runs applications made from more than one container.
One YAML file can hold service definitions together with network and volume settings.
The stack can be created and started together with `docker compose up`.
Compose provides lifecycle operations for starting, stopping, and rebuilding services.
You can inspect which services are running.
You can follow logs from the running services.
gotchas: A service can need time after its containers start before the application is ready. Wait and try again if it does not respond immediately.
`docker compose down` removes the containers and network but normally keeps volumes. Use `docker compose down --volumes` when the stored data should also be deleted.
Do not confuse the files: a Dockerfile builds an image, while a Compose file describes the containers that run.

docker compose up.summary: Build, create, start, and attach to Docker Compose service containers. Use detached mode to leave them running in the background.
docker compose up.explanation: Compose reads the application configuration, builds or pulls needed images, then creates or updates the service containers and starts them. Without `-d`, it combines container output in the terminal and stops the containers when the command ends; with `-d`, the containers continue running in the background.

parameters.name: SERVICE...
parameters.description: Optional service names to start. If omitted, Compose operates on all services in the application configuration.

parameters.name: OPTIONS
parameters.description: Command options, such as `--detach`, `--no-recreate`, `--force-recreate`, `--attach`, and `--no-attach`.

docker compose up.returns: Exit code 1 on an error. Ctrl+C or SIGTERM stops the containers and returns exit code 0.

example.title: Start a Compose application in the background
example.code:
docker compose up -d
# The services now run in the background.

docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f web
example.explanation: This starts every service in the Compose file without keeping the terminal attached. The later commands show service status and follow logs for only the web service.

useCases.title: Run all services interactively
useCases.scenario: Start the complete application defined in `compose.yaml` and watch its combined container output.

useCases.title: Run in detached mode
useCases.scenario: Start services for local development while keeping the terminal available for other commands.

useCases.title: Run selected services
useCases.scenario: Start only selected services when working on part of a Compose application.

useCases.title: Debug startup hooks
useCases.scenario: Inspect a failed `pre_start` hook before trying the service again.

interview.question: What does `docker compose up` do?
interview.answer: It builds or pulls required images, creates or recreates containers, starts services, and attaches to their combined output. Linked services are also started when needed.
interview.followUp: How can output from noisy services be excluded? Use `--no-attach` for those services, or use `--attach` to select the services whose output should be shown.

interview.question: When does Compose recreate an existing container?
interview.answer: A changed service configuration or image causes Compose to stop and recreate that service's container. Mounted volumes are preserved during this recreation.
interview.followUp: How can every container be recreated even without detected changes? Add `--force-recreate`.

interview.question: How do you keep the services running after the terminal command returns?
interview.answer: Use `docker compose up -d`. Detached mode starts the services in the background and leaves them running instead of attaching the terminal to their output.
interview.followUp: How can logs for one service be watched afterward? Run `docker compose logs -f SERVICE`, such as `docker compose logs -f web`.

keyPoints: The command can build images, create or recreate containers, start them, and attach the terminal to their output.
Starting one service also starts its linked services when those services are not already running.
Attached mode combines output from the containers, so you can watch the application in one terminal.
Use detached mode to start the application in the background and keep its containers running.
Use `--force-recreate` when all service containers must be stopped and recreated.
A failed pre-start hook stops startup and keeps its hook container available for inspection.
gotchas: Running `docker compose up` in attached mode does not leave the containers running after the command exits. Use `-d` when they should keep running.
Changed service configuration or images can cause existing containers to be stopped and recreated. Use `--no-recreate` to avoid that behavior.
Do not use `docker compose down -v` casually. Removing named volumes permanently deletes their stored data.
A command error returns exit code 1. An interruption with Ctrl+C or SIGTERM stops containers and returns 0.

docker exec.summary: Runs a new command in a running Docker container. Use options to control input, terminals, environment variables, users, privileges, and the working directory.
docker exec.explanation: The command starts a new process inside a running container. It uses the container's default working directory unless `--workdir` changes it. The process runs only while the container's main process is running. Use `sh -c` when you need shell features such as command chaining.

parameters.name: OPTIONS
parameters.description: Options that control the exec process, such as environment variables, input, terminal, user, and working directory.

parameters.name: CONTAINER
parameters.description: The name or ID of a running container.

parameters.name: COMMAND [ARG...]
parameters.description: The executable to run, followed by its arguments.

docker exec.returns: The command's result; in attached mode its output is shown, while detached mode runs it in the background.

example.title: Run a command in a container
example.code:
docker run --name mycontainer -d -i -t alpine /bin/sh
docker exec -it -w /root mycontainer pwd
example.explanation: Starts an Alpine container, then runs `pwd` in `/root` with an interactive terminal.

useCases.title: Interactive shell
useCases.scenario: Open a shell for inspection or manual work.

useCases.title: One-off container task
useCases.scenario: Run a one-time command, such as creating a file or checking a path.

useCases.title: Custom exec environment
useCases.scenario: Run a command with temporary variables or a different directory.

interview.question: What does `docker exec` do?
interview.answer: `docker exec` starts a new command process inside an already running container. It does not replace the container's primary process, and it works only while that primary process is running.
interview.followUp: What happens after the container restarts? The exec process is not restarted automatically.

interview.question: How do you open an interactive shell?
interview.answer: Use `-i` to keep standard input open and `-t` to allocate a pseudo-terminal. Together, `-it` is useful for an interactive shell such as `sh`.
interview.followUp: How would you run a command in the background? Add `-d` for detached mode.

interview.question: How can you choose the working directory?
interview.answer: The command runs in the container's default working directory unless `-w` or `--workdir` supplies another directory. The option accepts a path inside the container.
interview.followUp: What does `docker exec -it mycontainer pwd` print when no working directory was set? The documented example prints `/`.

keyPoints: It starts a separate command inside a container that is already running.
Use `-e` or `--env` to set or override variables for only the new exec process.
Environment variables set for an exec process are not added to other processes in the container.
Without `-w`, the command uses the working directory configured when the container was created.
Use `-d` or `--detach` when the command should run without attaching the terminal.
Use `--privileged` to give the exec command extended privileges.
gotchas: Pass an executable and its arguments. A quoted command string with shell operators does not run by itself; use `sh -c` for that.
The container's main process must still be running. An exec process is not restarted when the container restarts.
Unpause a paused container before using `docker exec`.

docker ps.explanation: This Swarm management command shows tasks on one or more nodes. Without a node argument, it uses the current node. Use filters to narrow the output, and use output options to change names, detail, formatting, or whether only task IDs appear.

parameters.description: Options such as filters, formatting, name resolution, truncation, and quiet output.

parameters.name: NODE...
parameters.description: One or more node names or IDs. If omitted, the current node is used.

docker ps.returns: A list of tasks and their states for the selected node or nodes.

example.title: List tasks on a node

example.explanation: Lists the tasks Docker knows about on the specified node.

useCases.title: Filter tasks

useCases.scenario: Get task IDs for scripts or further commands.
