useCases.scenario: You need structured data for scripts or reports.

interview.question: How does kubectl connect to a cluster?
interview.answer: kubectl sends commands to a Kubernetes cluster through the Kubernetes API. It normally uses $HOME/.kube/config, or another file selected with KUBECONFIG or --kubeconfig.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect the active context? Run kubectl config current-context, then use kubectl config get-contexts to list available contexts.

interview.question: What is the basic kubectl command structure?
interview.answer: The general form is kubectl command TYPE NAME flags. TYPE can be singular, plural, or an abbreviation, and names are case-sensitive.
interview.followUp: What happens when NAME is omitted? For commands such as kubectl get pods, kubectl returns all matching resources in the selected namespace.

interview.question: How do you inspect Kubernetes resources?
interview.answer: Use kubectl get to list resources, kubectl describe to show detailed state, and kubectl logs to print a container's logs. Output can be formatted with options such as -o yaml, -o json, or -o wide.
interview.followUp: How would you extract selected fields? Use -o jsonpath=<template>, or use custom-columns for a table of chosen fields.

keyPoints: kubectl communicates with the cluster control plane through the Kubernetes API.
The default kubeconfig file is $HOME/.kube/config.
Use KUBECONFIG or --kubeconfig to select other kubeconfig files.
Resource types accept singular, plural, and short forms without case sensitivity.
For multiple resources, provide resource names or manifest files.
Use -o or --output to choose a supported output format.
Without an output option, kubectl uses readable plain text.
gotchas: Command-line flags take precedence over defaults and matching environment variables.
Prefer YAML manifests for easier reading, especially when writing configuration files.
An explicit namespace flag overrides the namespace selected through POD_NAMESPACE.

kubectl apply.summary: kubectl apply creates or updates Kubernetes resources from YAML, JSON, standard input, or a Kustomize directory. It changes declared fields while leaving unspecified fields alone.
kubectl apply.explanation: kubectl apply reads a resource definition from a file, standard input, or a Kustomize directory. It creates missing resources and updates existing resources to reflect the fields declared in the configuration. Fields not declared locally remain unchanged.

parameters.name: -f FILENAME
parameters.description: Input file, directory, or - for standard input.

parameters.name: -k DIRECTORY
parameters.description: Directory containing kustomization.yaml.

parameters.name: -l, --selector
parameters.description: Select resources using a label selector.

parameters.name: --prune
parameters.description: Remove matching resources not declared in the configuration. This feature is alpha.

kubectl apply.returns: Creates or updates the declared Kubernetes resources. The command exits with a non-zero status when a warning is treated as an error.

example.title: Apply a file
example.code: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
example.explanation: This reads the YAML file and creates or updates the declared resource.

useCases.title: Manage a resource from a file
useCases.scenario: You keep a Deployment definition in a YAML file and want the cluster to match it.

useCases.title: Apply a Kustomize directory
useCases.scenario: Several resource definitions are assembled with kustomization.yaml.

useCases.title: Apply data from standard input
useCases.scenario: Another command generates JSON that should be sent directly to Kubernetes.

interview.question: What does kubectl apply do?
interview.answer: Use kubectl apply with -f followed by a file, directory, or standard input. It creates the resource when it does not exist and updates it when it does.
interview.followUp: How can you apply a Kustomize configuration? Use -k followed by the directory containing kustomization.yaml.

interview.question: What input formats and sources does apply support?
interview.answer: The command accepts YAML and JSON. A hyphen passed to -f tells kubectl to read the configuration from standard input.
interview.followUp: How would you apply JSON produced by another command? Pipe it to kubectl apply -f -.

interview.question: What happens to fields that are not in the configuration?
interview.answer: Apply changes only the fields declared in the local configuration. Other fields already set on the resource are left unchanged.
interview.followUp: How does apply handle resources that do not exist? It creates them from the declared configuration.

keyPoints: Use apply to create or update a resource from a file or from standard input.
The configuration can be written in either JSON or YAML.
The resource definition must identify the resource that apply should manage.
Apply merges configuration-owned values with values supplied by the cluster and can order dependent resources.
Fields absent from the local configuration are not changed by apply.
gotchas: Create the resource first with apply or with create --save-config. This preserves the configuration data that apply needs.
Do not use --prune casually. The documentation marks it as alpha and says it is not complete.

kubectl describe.summary: kubectl describe prints detailed information about one or more Kubernetes resources. It can also show related items, such as events and controllers.
kubectl describe.explanation: kubectl describe builds a detailed view of one or more Kubernetes resources. It can include related information, such as events and controllers, and can select resources by name, name prefix, label, file, or resource type.
kubectl describe.syntax: kubectl describe (-f FILENAME | TYPE [NAME_PREFIX | -l label] | TYPE/NAME)

parameters.name: --all-namespaces, -A
parameters.description: Show matching resources in every namespace.

parameters.name: --chunk-size
parameters.description: Set the size of returned list chunks. Use 0 to disable chunking.

parameters.name: --filename, -f
parameters.description: Read the resource from a file, directory, or URL.

parameters.name: --kustomize, -k
parameters.description: Process a kustomization directory.

parameters.name: --recursive, -R
parameters.description: Process the directory passed with --filename recursively.

parameters.name: --selector, -l
parameters.description: Filter resources with a label query.

kubectl describe.returns: Prints a detailed description of the selected Kubernetes resources.

example.title: Describe Kubernetes resources
example.code:
kubectl describe pod nginx
kubectl describe pods -l name=myLabel
kubectl describe -f pod.json
example.explanation: The first command shows one pod. The second shows pods with a label. The third reads the resource from a file.

useCases.title: Inspect a resource
useCases.scenario: Inspect one node or pod while troubleshooting.

useCases.title: Filter by label
useCases.scenario: Find resources with a known label.

useCases.title: Describe from a file
useCases.scenario: Review resources defined in a manifest.

useCases.title: Search all namespaces
useCases.scenario: Inspect resources across namespaces.

interview.question: What does kubectl describe do?
interview.answer: kubectl describe shows detailed state for one or more resources. It can also show related resources, such as events or controllers.
interview.followUp: Why can it make several API requests? It may gather related information, such as node events and pods running on that node, to build the description.

interview.question: How can resources be selected?
interview.answer: The command accepts a resource type with an optional name or name prefix, a label selector, a resource file, or a type/name form. Examples include pods/nginx and -f pod.json.
interview.followUp: How would you describe every pod with a label? Use kubectl describe pods -l name=myLabel.

interview.question: How does namespace selection work?
interview.answer: Use --all-namespaces, or -A, to list matching resources across all namespaces. The current context namespace is ignored when this flag is present.
interview.followUp: What happens if --all-namespaces is combined with a namespace setting? The explicit namespace setting does not control the search.

keyPoints: The output gives detailed resource information and can include related events or controllers.
You can select one object, all resources of a type, a name prefix, or resources matching a label.
Run kubectl api-resources to see supported resource types.
The chunk-size option controls how large resource lists are returned at one time.
gotchas: Do not combine --kustomize with --filename or --recursive.
With --all-namespaces, kubectl searches every namespace instead of using the current namespace.
A name argument is checked as an exact resource name before kubectl tries it as a name prefix.

kubectl exec.summary: Runs a command inside a container in a Kubernetes Pod. Use -- before the command, and use -c to select a container when needed.
kubectl exec.explanation: kubectl exec runs a command inside a container in a running Pod. Put the command after -- so kubectl does not treat the command's options as its own. Use -i and -t for an interactive terminal, and use -c when the Pod has multiple containers.

parameters.name: POD | TYPE/NAME
parameters.description: Pod or resource reference, such as POD or TYPE/NAME.

parameters.name: -c, --container
parameters.description: Container name. If omitted, kubectl selects the annotated default or first container.

parameters.name: -f, --filename
parameters.description: Files to use when executing into the resource.

parameters.name: --pod-running-timeout
parameters.description: Time to wait for a running Pod; default is 1 minute.

kubectl exec.returns: Command output is sent to the client. With interactive terminal options, input is sent to the container and its output is sent back.

example.title: Open a container shell
example.code: kubectl exec -i -t my-pod -c main-app -- /bin/bash
example.explanation: This opens an interactive Bash shell in the main-app container.

useCases.title: Run one command
useCases.scenario: Inspect a running container without opening a shell.

useCases.title: Open a shell
useCases.scenario: Work interactively inside a container.

useCases.title: Target a container
useCases.scenario: Choose one container in a multi-container Pod.

useCases.title: Use a resource target
useCases.scenario: Run a command through a resource reference such as a Deployment or Service.

interview.question: What does kubectl exec do?
interview.answer: kubectl exec runs a command inside a container in a Pod. The command follows --, which separates it from kubectl options.
interview.followUp: How would you run a command in a specific container? Add -c followed by the container name before --.

interview.question: How do you open an interactive shell?
interview.answer: Use -i or --stdin to pass input and -t or --tty to allocate a terminal. Together, they let you use an interactive shell.
interview.followUp: What command opens Bash interactively? Use kubectl exec -i -t POD -- /bin/bash.

interview.question: How do you choose the container?
interview.answer: For a Pod with multiple containers, specify the target with -c or --container. If omitted, kubectl uses the default-container annotation or the first container.
interview.followUp: What happens when no container is specified? kubectl chooses the annotated default container, or otherwise the first one.

keyPoints: Use kubectl exec to run a command inside a container.
The command accepts a Pod or a resource such as TYPE/NAME, followed by the command.
You can name the target container with -c or --container.
Without a selected container or annotation, kubectl uses the first container.
A non-interactive command can print environment variables from the container.
You can target a Deployment resource; kubectl runs the command in its first Pod.
gotchas: Use -- before the command and its arguments.
Do not let command flags be parsed as kubectl flags.
Do not quote the command unless you would normally run it quoted.

kubectl get.summary: `kubectl get` displays one or more Kubernetes resources. It supports resource filters and several output formats, including YAML, JSON, wide text, JSONPath, and custom columns.
kubectl get.explanation: kubectl get asks the Kubernetes API for one or more resources and prints their main details. You can select a resource type and optional name, label, file, namespace, or output format.

parameters.name: TYPE
parameters.description: Resource type, optionally including API version and group.

parameters.name: NAME or resource input
parameters.description: Optional resource name, type/name, label selector, file, or kustomization directory.

parameters.name: --output, -o
parameters.description: Output format, such as json, yaml, wide, jsonpath, or custom-columns.

parameters.name: --selector, -l
parameters.description: Label selector used to filter resources.

parameters.name: --sort-by
parameters.description: JSONPath expression used to sort supported results.

kubectl get.returns: A table or selected representation of one or more Kubernetes resources.

example.title: List pods and print one as YAML
example.code:
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl get pod web-pod-13je7 -o yaml
example.explanation: The first command lists pods with extra details, such as the node name. The second prints one pod as YAML.

useCases.title: Inspect cluster resources
useCases.scenario: Check pods, services, deployments, or other resources in a namespace.

useCases.title: Extract selected fields
useCases.scenario: Read exact fields such as a pod phase or container image.

useCases.title: Format command output
useCases.scenario: Create stable, script-friendly tables or structured output.

useCases.title: Filter resource lists
useCases.scenario: Find resources matching labels or field conditions.

interview.question: What does kubectl get do?
interview.answer: kubectl get displays one or more Kubernetes resources. It can filter results with a label selector and can format output as JSON, YAML, wide text, JSONPath, templates, or custom columns.
interview.followUp: How would you select only running pods? Use a field selector such as `kubectl get pods --field-selector status.phase=Running`.

interview.question: How can kubectl get identify resources?
interview.answer: The command accepts a resource type and optional name, a type/name form, a file, or a kustomization directory. If no name is given, it lists all matching resources in the selected scope.
interview.followUp: How can you read a resource from a manifest without naming it? Use `kubectl get -f pod.yaml -o json`.

interview.question: How can you control and sort kubectl get output?
interview.answer: Use `-o` or `--output` to choose the result format. Common formats include `json`, `yaml`, `name`, `wide`, `jsonpath`, and `custom-columns`.
interview.followUp: How can you sort the results? Add `--sort-by` with a JSONPath field, such as `.metadata.name`.

keyPoints: The default output is a table containing the main information for the selected resources.
Use `--selector` or `-l` to return resources matching labels.
Run `kubectl api-resources` to discover resource types that the cluster supports.
Go templates can extract chosen fields from returned resources.
Use `-k` with a directory containing `kustomization.yaml` to get generated resources.
gotchas: For namespaced resources, the command uses the current namespace unless you choose another namespace.
Resource type names are flexible, but resource names are case-sensitive.
Command-line flags take priority over defaults and matching environment variables.

kubectl logs.summary: Print logs for a container in a pod or supported resource. You can stream logs, choose a container, read previous logs, or limit the output.
kubectl logs.explanation: kubectl logs requests container output from a pod or another supported resource. Choose a container with -c, stream new output with -f, select an earlier terminated container with -p, or filter the amount and age of output with options such as --tail and --since.

parameters.name: -f, --follow
parameters.description: Follow log output as it arrives.

parameters.name: -p, --previous
parameters.description: Read logs from the previous terminated container.

parameters.name: -c, --container
parameters.description: Select a container by name.

parameters.name: --all-containers
parameters.description: Include logs from all containers.

parameters.name: --limit-bytes
parameters.description: Limit returned log bytes.

parameters.name: --tail
parameters.description: Return only the newest requested number of lines.

parameters.name: --since
parameters.description: Return logs from the specified recent time period.

parameters.name: --pod-running-timeout
parameters.description: Wait for at least one pod to run for the specified duration.

kubectl logs.returns: Log output from the selected pod, container, or supported resource.

example.title: Read current, streaming, and previous logs
example.code:
kubectl logs nginx --tail=20
kubectl logs -f -c app nginx
kubectl logs -p -c app nginx
example.explanation: The first command shows the newest 20 lines. The second streams logs from the app container. The third shows logs from its previous terminated instance.

useCases.title: Debug a container
useCases.scenario: Inspect a pod after an error or failed startup.

useCases.title: Stream live logs
useCases.scenario: Watch new application output while testing a change.

useCases.title: Read previous logs
useCases.scenario: Find output from a container that restarted.

useCases.title: Review logs by label
useCases.scenario: Collect limited output from several matching pods.

interview.question: How do you select which container logs to print?
interview.answer: Use `kubectl logs POD` for a pod with one container. Use `kubectl logs POD -c CONTAINER` when selecting a specific container, or `--all-containers=true` for every container.
interview.followUp: How do you read logs from a deployment? Use a resource form such as `kubectl logs deployment/nginx`; `--all-pods=true` requests logs from all pods in that deployment.

interview.question: How do you stream logs?
interview.answer: Add `-f` or `--follow` to keep the command streaming new log output. Add `--ignore-errors=true` when errors during following should not stop the stream.
interview.followUp: How can you reduce the amount of output? Use `--tail=20`, `--limit-bytes=500`, or `--since=1h` for the relevant limit or time window.

interview.question: How do you inspect logs from a previous container instance?
interview.answer: Use `-p` or `--previous` to request logs from the previous terminated container instance. Include `-c CONTAINER` when the pod has multiple containers.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect many matching pods? Use `-l app=nginx`, and for concurrent requests set `--max-log-requests=10`.

keyPoints: The command prints logs for a pod or for a supported resource such as a deployment or job.
Use `-f` to keep receiving log lines instead of taking a one-time snapshot.
Use `--all-containers=true` when output from every container is needed.
Use `--limit-bytes` to cap the returned output by size; zero means no limit.
`--pod-running-timeout` can wait for a pod to start before logs are requested.
A deployment target can be combined with `--all-pods=true` to request logs from all its pods.
gotchas: For a pod with several containers, provide -c CONTAINER unless you request all containers.
--ignore-errors applies when following logs and lets the stream continue after errors.
Avoid --insecure-skip-tls-verify-backend unless needed for an expired kubelet certificate; it weakens identity verification.

kubectl port-forward.summary: kubectl port-forward sends TCP traffic from one or more local ports to a selected pod. You can choose a fixed local port or let kubectl allocate one.
kubectl port-forward.explanation: kubectl port-forward opens a local listening port and sends its TCP traffic to a port on a selected pod. You can select a pod directly or use a Deployment, ReplicaSet, or Service; kubectl chooses a matching pod when needed.

parameters.name: TYPE/NAME
parameters.description: Resource type and name used to select the target pod, such as `pod/mypod` or `deployment/mydeployment`.

parameters.name: [LOCAL_PORT:]REMOTE_PORT
parameters.description: Local port, optionally followed by a colon and the remote pod port. A blank local port requests automatic allocation.

parameters.name: --address
parameters.description: Addresses on which kubectl listens. Values are comma-separated IP addresses or `localhost`; default is `localhost`.

kubectl port-forward.returns: The command keeps the forwarding session open and prints the local and remote endpoints. It ends when the selected pod terminates or the session is stopped.

example.title: Forward a local port
example.code: kubectl port-forward deployment/myapp 8080:80
example.explanation: This sends requests from local port 8080 to port 80 on a pod selected by the Deployment.

useCases.title: Debug a database
useCases.scenario: Access a database running in a pod from a local database client.

useCases.title: Test an internal service
useCases.scenario: Test an application without exposing it through an external load balancer.

useCases.title: Allocate a free local port
useCases.scenario: Avoid choosing a local port that another process already uses.

interview.question: What does kubectl port-forward do?
interview.answer: The command creates a local listener and forwards TCP traffic to a selected pod. Its basic form is `kubectl port-forward TYPE/NAME [LOCAL_PORT:]REMOTE_PORT`.
interview.followUp: What happens if the selected pod terminates? The session ends, and the command must be run again.

interview.question: Which resources can select the target pod?
interview.answer: You can specify a resource such as a pod, Deployment, ReplicaSet, or Service. If more than one pod matches, kubectl selects one automatically.
interview.followUp: How can you avoid a fixed local port? Use a form such as `:27017`; kubectl chooses an available local port.

interview.question: How do you control the local listening address?
interview.answer: The default listen address is localhost. Use `--address` with IP addresses or localhost to choose where kubectl listens.
interview.followUp: What protocol is supported? The documented command supports TCP ports only, not UDP.

keyPoints: The command connects one or more local ports to ports on a pod.
A resource name without a type is treated as a pod name.
A selector such as a Deployment can result in kubectl choosing one matching pod.
Use `--address` with a comma-separated list of listening addresses.
Leave the local port empty, such as `:5000`, to let kubectl choose it.
With a Service, a named service port can be used as the remote port.
gotchas: Forwarding stops when the selected pod ends. Run the command again to resume it.
This command forwards TCP traffic only. It does not support UDP.
Access is controlled by Kubernetes authorization, such as RBAC, and enforced by the API server.
The command keeps running while the forwarding session is active, so use another terminal for other commands.

kubectl rollout.summary: `kubectl rollout status` shows rollout progress for a resource. It watches the latest revision by default and can instead watch a chosen revision or return immediately.
kubectl rollout.explanation: `kubectl rollout status` watches the latest rollout of a resource and reports its progress until it finishes. You can stop waiting, set a timeout, filter resources with a label selector, or watch a chosen revision.

parameters.name: resource
parameters.description: Resource type and name, written as `TYPE NAME` or `TYPE/NAME`.

parameters.name: --revision
parameters.description: Select a specific rollout revision; the default is the latest revision.

parameters.name: --watch
parameters.description: Set whether to watch until the rollout finishes. Defaults to true.

parameters.name: --timeout
parameters.description: Maximum time to wait; zero means no limit.

parameters.name: --selector
parameters.description: Filter resources by a label query.

kubectl rollout.returns: Shows rollout status and exits when the rollout finishes, watching is disabled, or the timeout is reached.

example.title: Watch a Deployment rollout
example.code: kubectl rollout status deployment/nginx --timeout=5m
example.explanation: Watches the nginx Deployment until its rollout finishes, or stops after five minutes.

useCases.title: Verify a Deployment update
useCases.scenario: After changing a Deployment, wait until its new Pods are ready.

useCases.title: Run a non-blocking check
useCases.scenario: In a script, check current status without blocking.

useCases.title: Track a fixed revision
useCases.scenario: Monitor one revision while preventing a newer rollout from taking over.

interview.question: What does `kubectl rollout status` do?
interview.answer: It watches the rollout status of a resource, such as a Deployment, and normally waits until the rollout completes. The default behavior watches the latest revision.
interview.followUp: How can you avoid waiting? Use `--watch=false`, or set `--timeout` to stop waiting after a duration.

interview.question: How do you make rollout status return without waiting?
interview.answer: Use `--watch=false` when the command should report the current status without waiting for completion. The default for `--watch` is true.
interview.followUp: What happens if a new rollout starts during the watch? The command follows the latest revision unless `--revision` pins a specific one.

interview.question: What resource forms and filters does the command support?
interview.answer: The command accepts a resource in the form `TYPE NAME` or `TYPE/NAME`, such as `deployment/nginx`. It can also select resources with `--selector`.
interview.followUp: How can you limit how long a watch runs? Use a duration such as `--timeout=2m`; zero means no timeout.

keyPoints: The command reports the progress of a resource rollout.
Provide a resource as separate type and name values or as `TYPE/NAME`.
Set `--watch=false` to return without waiting for completion.
Use `--revision=N` to watch one particular revision.
`--timeout` controls how long the status watch can run; zero means no limit.
Use `--selector` to filter resources by labels.
gotchas: The command waits for the latest rollout by default.
Use `--revision` when another rollout must not replace the revision being watched.

kubectl scale.summary: `kubectl scale` sets the desired replica count for a Deployment, ReplicaSet, ReplicationController, or StatefulSet. It can check preconditions before sending the scale request.
kubectl scale.explanation: The command changes the desired replica count of a Deployment, ReplicaSet, ReplicationController, or StatefulSet. Kubernetes then creates or removes Pods so the workload moves toward that count. You can add a precondition to require a specific current replica count before the change is sent.

parameters.name: --replicas
parameters.description: The target replica count.

parameters.name: --current-replicas
parameters.description: Require the current replica count to match this value.

parameters.name: --resource-version
parameters.description: Require the resource version to match this value.

parameters.name: --all
parameters.description: Select all matching resources in the namespace.

parameters.name: --dry-run
parameters.description: Use a client or server dry run, or perform the operation normally.

parameters.name: -f, --filename
parameters.description: Read the resource from one or more manifest files.

kubectl scale.returns: On success, kubectl reports that the resource was scaled. The command changes the resource's desired replica count; Kubernetes then reconciles the Pods.

example.title: Scale a Deployment
example.code:
kubectl scale deployment/nginx-deployment --replicas=4
kubectl get deployment nginx-deployment
example.explanation: Sets the Deployment to four replicas, then checks its replica count.

useCases.title: Scale up a workload
useCases.scenario: Traffic is expected to increase.

useCases.title: Scale down a workload
useCases.scenario: Demand or resource use is lower.

useCases.title: Scale a Deployment to zero
useCases.scenario: A workload should pause without deleting its configuration.

useCases.title: Scale multiple resources
useCases.scenario: Several matching resources need the same replica count.

interview.question: How do you scale a Deployment?
interview.answer: Use `kubectl scale deployment/name --replicas=COUNT`. The command sets the desired replica count, and the Deployment creates or removes Pods to reach it.
interview.followUp: How can you avoid scaling an unexpectedly changed Deployment? Add `--current-replicas=COUNT` or `--resource-version=VERSION` as a precondition.

interview.question: What does `--current-replicas` do?
interview.answer: Use `--current-replicas=COUNT`. Kubernetes checks that the resource still has that many replicas before sending the scale request.
interview.followUp: What happens when the check fails? The scale request is not attempted because the precondition is no longer true.

interview.question: How can you preview a scale operation?
interview.answer: Use `--dry-run=client` to print the object that would be sent without sending it. Use `--dry-run=server` to submit a server-side request without saving the resource.
interview.followUp: Which dry-run value is the default? `none`, which performs the normal operation.

keyPoints: `kubectl scale` changes the desired size of a Deployment, ReplicaSet, or ReplicationController.
Use preconditions when the scale should occur only if the resource is still in an expected state.
A StatefulSet can be scaled by naming it and supplying the desired replica count.
`--all` selects every matching resource in the current namespace.
Client dry-run shows the object locally and does not send a request to the cluster.
Server dry-run sends the request for server validation but does not persist the resource.
gotchas: A precondition can stop the scale if the current replica count or resource version does not match.
Scaling a Deployment to zero stops its Pods but does not delete the Deployment or ReplicaSet.
Scaling down does not immediately remove Pods; termination follows the Pod's grace-period setting.

Kubernetes.summary: A Kubernetes Service gives a stable network endpoint to one or more Pods. It hides changing Pod IP addresses and routes client traffic to the current matching backends.
Kubernetes.explanation: A Service gives a stable network endpoint to a changing group of Pods. A selector finds matching Pods, and Kubernetes updates the Service's backing endpoints as Pods are created or removed. Clients can use the Service instead of tracking individual Pod IP addresses.
Kubernetes.syntax:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: <service-name>
spec:
  selector: <label-selector>
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: <service-port>
      targetPort: <pod-port>

parameters.name: spec.selector
parameters.description: Selects the Pods that provide the Service backend.

parameters.name: spec.ports
parameters.description: Defines the client-facing port, protocol, and destination port.

parameters.name: spec.type
parameters.description: Chooses how the Service is exposed, such as ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, or ExternalName.

parameters.name: spec.ports[].appProtocol
parameters.description: Specifies the application protocol hint for a Service port.

Kubernetes.returns: A Service object with a stable network endpoint and routing to its selected backends.

example.title: Expose matching Pods
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-service
spec:
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: MyApp
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 9376
example.explanation: This Service sends traffic on port 80 to port 9376 on matching Pods.

useCases.scenario: A Deployment creates and removes Pods while a frontend needs a stable backend address.

useCases.title: Route web traffic with Ingress
useCases.scenario: Several application components need one external HTTP entry point.

useCases.title: Represent external backends
useCases.scenario: Some backends run outside Kubernetes or are being moved into the cluster.

useCases.title: Expose a Service externally
useCases.scenario: A client must reach an application from outside the cluster.

Kubernetes.since: v1.20 for stable appProtocol; EndpointSlices are documented

interview.question: What problem does a Service solve?
interview.answer: A Service is an abstraction that exposes one or more Pods through a network endpoint. A selector usually chooses the Pods, so clients do not need to know their changing IP addresses.
interview.followUp: How does Kubernetes keep the backend list current? It updates EndpointSlices when the Pods selected by the Service change.

interview.question: Compare the main Service types.
interview.answer: ClusterIP exposes the Service only inside the cluster and is the default type. NodePort exposes a fixed port on each Node, while LoadBalancer uses an external load balancer.
interview.followUp: What does Kubernetes provide for LoadBalancer itself? Kubernetes does not directly provide the load-balancing component; a provider or integration must supply it.

interview.question: When would you create a Service without a selector?
interview.answer: A Service without a selector can still route traffic when matching EndpointSlice objects are provided. This allows backends outside the cluster or during a migration to be represented.
interview.followUp: Can kubectl port-forward such a Service? No. The API server rejects proxying to endpoints that are not mapped to Pods.

keyPoints: A Service is a Kubernetes API object. You can create, inspect, and change it through the API, often with kubectl.
The Service controller watches for matching Pods and keeps the Service's backend set aligned with them.
A ClusterIP gives the Service a virtual internal IP that clients can use instead of Pod IPs.
A Service can send traffic to a named container port, so backend port numbers can change without changing clients.
Selectors are the usual way to connect a Service to its Pods.
The appProtocol field gives implementations a hint about the protocol used by a Service port.
gotchas: The default protocol is TCP. A Service can use another supported protocol when needed.
Every port needs a name when one Service defines multiple ports.
Port forwarding through the API server does not work for a Service without a selector.

kustomize.summary: A Kustomization file tells Kustomize which Kubernetes resources to include and how to generate, transform, or validate them. It supports reusable bases and overlays for environment-specific changes without editing the base files.
kustomize.explanation: Kustomize reads resources, then runs generators, transformers, and validators in that order. A directory resource can contain another kustomization.yaml, so Kustomize builds that directory first and uses its objects as input. Fields such as namePrefix and patches provide shorter configuration for common transformations.
kustomize.syntax:
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - path-or-url

example.title: A small overlay
example.code:
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - deployment.yaml
  - service.yaml
namePrefix: dev-
patches:
  - path: replicas.yaml
example.explanation: This overlay includes two resource files, adds a name prefix, and applies a patch.

useCases.title: Environment overlays
useCases.scenario: Keep shared Kubernetes YAML unchanged while adding environment-specific patches.

useCases.title: Manifest generation
useCases.scenario: Build final Kubernetes YAML from several resource files and generators.

useCases.title: Resource-wide changes
useCases.scenario: Apply consistent names or labels across a group of resources.

interview.question: What is the processing order in a Kustomize build?
interview.answer: Kustomize builds a resource list from resources, adds generated objects, transforms the list, and then validates it. This gives the build a defined processing order.
interview.followUp: What happens when a resource points to a directory? Kustomize recursively builds the directory's kustomization and inserts its resulting objects into the parent list.

interview.question: What are bases and overlays?
interview.answer: An overlay is a kustomization that refers to a base and applies changes such as patches. The base can remain unchanged while different overlays create variants such as development or production.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful with source control? Upstream base files can be updated separately, while owned overlays keep environment-specific changes.

interview.question: How do generators and transformers differ?
interview.answer: A generator creates resources from its own configuration and returns a resource map. A transformer receives the current resource map and can modify it, including adding, replacing, or removing resources.
interview.followUp: Can a transformer add resources? Yes. The resource map supports operations such as append, replace, remove, and clear.

keyPoints: A kustomization.yaml file describes how to create or change Kubernetes resource objects.
A resource entry may name a YAML file, a local directory, or a directory in a remote Git repository.
Use `kustomize build` to emit YAML, then pipe it to `kubectl apply -f -`.
Kustomize changes template-free YAML and leaves the original resource files usable without the customization.
Use overlays to maintain environment variants from a shared base.
The namePrefix field adds a prefix to resource names and references.
gotchas: Keep entries in the required order when list order affects the result.
Generators run after resources, while transformers and validators run later.
The core file also has fields beyond the four main lists; those fields are convenience forms.

Kustomize.summary: Build Kubernetes resource YAML from a kustomization.yaml file. The input can be a local directory or a Git URL.
Kustomize.explanation: Kustomize builds Kubernetes resources from a kustomization.yaml file. kubectl kustomize prints the generated YAML, while kubectl apply -k sends the generated resources to the cluster.

parameters.name: DIR
parameters.description: Directory containing kustomization.yaml, or a Git repository URL with a path suffix. Defaults to the current directory.

Kustomize.returns: The generated Kubernetes resource YAML is written to standard output, unless an output path is specified.

example.title: Render and apply a kustomization
example.code:
kubectl kustomize ./app
kubectl apply -k ./app
example.explanation: The first command renders the resources. The second command applies them to the cluster.

useCases.title: Preview resources
useCases.scenario: Inspect generated YAML before sending it to a cluster.

useCases.title: Use a remote base
useCases.scenario: Build configuration from shared files stored in a Git repository.

useCases.title: Customize resources
useCases.scenario: Create ConfigMaps or Secrets and change names, labels, images, or fields.

interview.question: What does kubectl kustomize do?
interview.answer: kubectl kustomize builds resources from a directory or Git URL that contains kustomization.yaml. It prints the resulting YAML instead of applying it.
interview.followUp: How would you apply the result? Use kubectl apply -k followed by the kustomization directory.

interview.question: What can a kustomization file contain?
interview.answer: A kustomization.yaml file can list resources and generators. Kustomize combines those inputs and applies configured transformations, such as labels, name prefixes, patches, and image changes.
interview.followUp: Why use generated names for ConfigMaps and Secrets? A content hash in the name changes when the data changes, helping trigger updates.

interview.question: What inputs can kubectl kustomize build?
interview.answer: The command accepts a local directory or a Git repository URL with a path relative to the repository root. If no directory is given, it uses the current directory.
interview.followUp: What risk comes with LoadRestrictionsNone? A configuration can depend on files outside its root, so moving it may break it.

keyPoints: The command reads kustomization.yaml and builds the Kubernetes resources it describes.
A local input must point to a directory that contains the kustomization file.
A Git URL can identify a kustomization in a repository subdirectory.
Use kubectl apply -k when the built resources should be sent to the cluster.
Generators create ConfigMaps and Secrets from files or literal key-value pairs.
The patches field supports strategic-merge and JSON 6902 patch styles.
gotchas: Without a directory argument, kubectl kustomize uses the current directory.
Using LoadRestrictionsNone allows files outside the kustomization root, but makes the configuration less portable.
Loading files outside the root can stop the kustomization from working after it is moved.

Linkerd.summary: Linkerd adds lightweight proxies to Kubernetes pods and uses a control plane for telemetry and runtime signals. Its CLI installs the control plane, injects proxies into selected services, and helps diagnose failures.
Linkerd.explanation: Linkerd adds a proxy to each selected application pod. The proxy sends telemetry to Linkerd's control plane and receives signals from it. The CLI can install the control plane, modify Kubernetes manifests with data-plane proxies, and inspect service behavior without changing application code.
Linkerd.syntax:
linkerd install | kubectl apply -f -
linkerd inject <manifest>
linkerd check --pre
linkerd check

example.title: Install and inject Linkerd
example.code:
curl https://run.linkerd.io/emojivoto.yml | kubectl apply -f -
linkerd check --pre
linkerd install | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl get -n emojivoto deploy/web -o yaml | linkerd inject - | kubectl apply -f -
linkerd check
example.explanation: This installs the demo app, checks the cluster, installs Linkerd, adds its proxy to the web Deployment, and checks the installation.

useCases.title: Observe a service
useCases.scenario: Add service telemetry without editing application code.

useCases.title: Debug runtime errors
useCases.scenario: Find which dependency causes request failures.

useCases.title: Introduce a sidecar safely
useCases.scenario: Apply proxy injection to one Deployment during a rolling update.

useCases.title: Use CLI diagnostics
useCases.scenario: Inspect service behavior from the terminal.

interview.question: What is Linkerd and how does it work?
interview.answer: Linkerd is a service sidecar and a service mesh. It adds lightweight proxies to pods, while a control plane provides telemetry and signals. This works without application code changes.
interview.followUp: How can Linkerd be added during live traffic? Inject the Deployment manifest and reapply it. Kubernetes performs a rolling update, replacing pods one at a time.

interview.question: How do you install and validate Linkerd?
interview.answer: Run `linkerd check --pre` before installation to find cluster problems. Then run `linkerd install | kubectl apply -f -` to generate and apply the control-plane manifest. Run `linkerd check` afterward to validate the installation.
interview.followUp: Why inspect the generated manifest? Both `linkerd install` and `linkerd inject` are text operations, so the YAML can be reviewed before applying it.

interview.question: How would you debug a failing service with Linkerd?
interview.answer: Inject only the service that should use Linkerd. The tutorial injects the `web` Deployment with `kubectl get ... -o yaml | linkerd inject - | kubectl apply -f -`. The dashboard then shows metrics for that service and its dependencies.
interview.followUp: How can the CLI replace the dashboard? Use `linkerd top`, `linkerd stat`, and `linkerd tap` for runtime inspection and debugging.

keyPoints: Linkerd can run beside a Kubernetes service and add runtime debugging, diagnostics, and reliability features.
The data-plane proxies send metrics to Linkerd's control plane and receive instructions from it.
Applications can use Linkerd without changing their source code.
`linkerd inject` changes a Kubernetes manifest as text, so you can inspect the result before applying it.
The Linkerd dashboard can display services in the Emojivoto namespace, including services that do not yet have a proxy.
gotchas: A running pod does not prove that the application is working. Use Linkerd metrics and request inspection to find runtime failures.
GKE clusters with RBAC enabled need an additional cluster-admin binding before installing certain telemetry features.
A missing server version means the control plane is not installed yet; install it before using server-side Linkerd features.

Loki.sourceTitle: Observe service mesh on Docker containers
Loki.summary: Loki is a log aggregation system. In the documented Docker setup, containers send logs to Loki through Docker's Loki logging driver, and Grafana uses Loki as a log data source.
Loki.explanation: Loki collects logs from Docker containers. Docker uses the Loki logging driver to send container logs to a Loki service, which Grafana can query as a data source.

example.title: Install the Loki Docker logging driver
example.code: docker plugin install grafana/loki-docker-driver:latest --alias loki --grant-all-permissions
example.explanation: Install the Docker plugin that lets Docker containers send logs to Loki.

useCases.title: Container log collection
useCases.scenario: Collect logs from Docker containers in a local service mesh setup.

useCases.title: Log exploration
useCases.scenario: Search and view service logs in Grafana.

useCases.title: Log-to-trace navigation
useCases.scenario: Connect logs with distributed traces.

interview.question: What is Loki used for?
interview.answer: Loki is a log aggregation system. In the documented Docker setup, containers send logs through the Loki Docker logging driver, and Grafana reads them from Loki.
interview.followUp: How would you connect Loki to Grafana? Configure a Grafana data source with type Loki and set its URL to the Loki service, such as http://loki:3100.

interview.question: How does Docker send logs to Loki?
interview.answer: Install the Loki Docker driver, then configure a container's logging driver and Loki URL. The driver sends container logs to the Loki service.
interview.followUp: What must be checked if logs do not arrive? Verify that the plugin is installed, the Loki URL is reachable, and the Loki service is exposed on the expected port.

interview.question: How does Grafana read logs from Loki?
interview.answer: Grafana uses a Loki data source to query logs. The documented configuration uses proxy access and points the data source URL at the Loki container on port 3100.
interview.followUp: How can logs link to traces? Configure a derived field that extracts a trace ID from log text and points it to the Tempo data source.

keyPoints: Loki stores and aggregates application logs for later searching and viewing.
A common observability setup uses Prometheus for metrics, Loki for logs, and Tempo for traces.
The Loki service must be reachable by the systems that send it logs.
Grafana can define Loki as a proxy data source for an organization.
gotchas: The example setup is for learning and testing. Review security settings before using it in production.
Containers cannot emit logs through this method until the Loki Docker logging driver is installed.

multi-stage build.summary: Multi-stage builds split a Dockerfile into separate stages. Build in one stage, then copy only runtime files into the final stage to keep the image smaller.
multi-stage build.explanation: A multi-stage Dockerfile has several build stages. Each stage starts with FROM. One stage can compile or package the application, while a later stage copies only the files needed at runtime. Build tools and temporary files stay out of the final image.
multi-stage build.returns: A final image containing the files copied into its last stage.

example.title: Build a small Go image
example.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM golang:1.26 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY <<'EOF' main.go
package main
import "fmt"
func main() { fmt.Println("hello, world") }
EOF
RUN go build -o /bin/hello ./main.go

FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /bin/hello /bin/hello
CMD ["/bin/hello"]
example.explanation: The first stage builds the program. The second stage contains only the compiled binary.

useCases.title: Compile without shipping the compiler
useCases.scenario: Compiled applications

useCases.title: Keep build tools out of the runtime image
useCases.scenario: Production images

useCases.title: Create separate debug, test, and production targets
useCases.scenario: Development workflows

interview.question: What is a multi-stage build, and why use one?
interview.answer: A multi-stage build uses multiple FROM instructions. Each FROM starts a new stage, and COPY --from transfers selected artifacts into a later stage. This keeps compilers and other build files out of the production image.
interview.followUp: How can a build select only one stage? Use docker build --target followed by the stage name. BuildKit builds only the dependencies of that target.

interview.question: How do you copy output between stages?
interview.answer: Name a stage by adding AS name to its FROM instruction, then refer to it with COPY --from=name. This is easier to maintain than numeric stage indexes.
interview.followUp: Can COPY --from use a source outside the Dockerfile? Yes. It can copy from a local image or an image tag or ID available through a registry.

interview.question: How does BuildKit change target-stage builds?
interview.answer: The legacy builder processes all stages before the selected target, even when some are unrelated. BuildKit skips stages that the target does not depend on.
interview.followUp: If stage2 depends on base but not stage1, which stages does BuildKit process? It processes base and stage2 and skips stage1.

keyPoints: Every FROM starts a separate stage, and stages may use different base images.
Copy only runtime artifacts into the final stage to produce a smaller image.
Use AS with a stage name so later instructions can refer to that stage.
A final stage based on scratch can contain only the application binary when the binary needs no extra runtime files.
COPY --from can take an external image as its source.
gotchas: Unnamed stages use numbers starting at 0. Names are clearer and keep COPY references stable when stages change.
With BuildKit, unrelated stages are skipped when you build a selected target. This can make targeted builds faster.
COPY --from can use an external image, not only an earlier stage. The required image may be downloaded during the build.

Namespace.summary: Kubernetes namespaces isolate groups of namespaced resources within one cluster. Names must be unique inside a namespace, but the same name can be used in other namespaces.
Namespace.explanation: A namespace groups namespaced Kubernetes objects inside one cluster. Resource names must be unique within that namespace, but the same name can be used in another namespace. Namespaces do not contain cluster-wide objects, and one resource cannot belong to more than one namespace.
Namespace.syntax:
kubectl get namespaces
kubectl get pods --namespace=<namespace-name>
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<namespace-name>

parameters.name: namespace
parameters.description: Namespace name used to scope a resource or kubectl request.

parameters.name: metadata.name
parameters.description: Name of the namespace resource.

Namespace.returns: A Namespace object when the API creates, reads, or updates one; a NamespaceList when it lists namespaces.

example.title: Create and use a namespace
example.code:
kubectl create namespace team-a
kubectl run nginx --image=nginx --namespace=team-a
kubectl get pods --namespace=team-a
example.explanation: This creates a namespace, starts a Pod in it, and lists Pods from that namespace.

useCases.title: Team separation
useCases.scenario: Many teams share one cluster and need separate resource names and management boundaries.

useCases.title: Resource quotas
useCases.scenario: An administrator needs to limit how many resources or how much CPU and memory a group can use.

useCases.title: Environment separation
useCases.scenario: The same application configuration must work in Development, Staging, and Production.

interview.question: What does a Kubernetes namespace isolate?
interview.answer: A namespace scopes namespaced objects such as Deployments and Services. Names may repeat in different namespaces, but each name must be unique inside its namespace. Cluster-wide objects such as Nodes and PersistentVolumes are not in a namespace.
interview.followUp: Does a namespace by itself secure a tenant? No. Use access controls, quotas, network policies, and other isolation settings as needed.

interview.question: How do you select a namespace with kubectl?
interview.answer: Use the --namespace flag for one kubectl request. To save a namespace for later commands in the current context, use kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<name>.
interview.followUp: How can you check the saved setting? Run kubectl config view --minify and inspect the namespace field.

interview.question: How does a namespace affect Service DNS?
interview.answer: A Service gets a DNS name in the form <service-name>.<namespace-name>.svc.cluster.local. A Pod using only the Service name resolves the Service in its local namespace; cross-namespace access needs the fully qualified name.
interview.followUp: Why must namespace names follow DNS label rules? Kubernetes uses them as part of Service DNS names.

keyPoints: Two namespaces can contain resources with the same name.
Namespaces are flat, and a namespaced resource belongs to one namespace only.
Resource quotas can divide and limit resource use between users or teams.
A new cluster starts with default, kube-node-lease, kube-public, and kube-system.
Namespace names must follow RFC 1123 DNS label rules.
Kubernetes adds an immutable label whose value is the namespace name.
gotchas: Do not create names beginning with kube-. Kubernetes reserves that prefix for system namespaces.
Use labels instead of separate namespaces when you only need to distinguish small variations of resources.
A namespace alone does not provide complete network isolation. Configure NetworkPolicy when Pods must be separated.
For production, create dedicated namespaces instead of putting workloads in default.

interview.question: How do you enable New Relic metric streaming?
interview.answer: Enable streaming from the cluster Overview page's Metrics view. Choose New Relic, then enter the New Relic Account ID and Ingest License Key.
interview.followUp: What access is needed? An HCP account with the Admin role and New Relic permission to retrieve the Ingest License Key are required.

interview.question: Which clusters support metric streaming?

interview.followUp: Can a Development tier cluster use this feature? No. It must be moved to an eligible production-grade tier.

Development tier clusters cannot use metrics streaming.

Nginx.summary: A Kubernetes Service gives a stable network address to a group of Pods. It selects Pods by labels and sends traffic to their target port.
Nginx.explanation: A Service gives a changing group of matching Pods one stable network address. Kubernetes selects Pods by labels, sends traffic to their target port, and updates the backing EndpointSlices when Pods are added or removed.
Nginx.syntax:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: <service-name>
spec:
  ports:
  - port: <service-port>
    targetPort: <pod-port>
    protocol: TCP
  selector:
    <label-key>: <label-value>

parameters.name: spec.ports[].port
parameters.description: Port exposed by the Service for clients.

parameters.name: spec.ports[].targetPort
parameters.description: Port accepted by each selected Pod; it may be a name or a number.

parameters.name: spec.selector
parameters.description: Label rule used to choose the backing Pods.

Nginx.returns: A Kubernetes Service object with a stable cluster IP and traffic routing to selected Pods.

example.title: Expose Pods with a Service
example.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx-service
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 8000
    targetPort: 80
    protocol: TCP
  selector:
    app: nginx
example.explanation: This Service sends TCP traffic on port 8000 to port 80 on Pods labeled app: nginx.

useCases.title: Load-balance traffic across replicas
useCases.scenario: Several replicated Pods provide the same application.

useCases.title: Provide a stable internal address
useCases.scenario: Pods need to reach an application without tracking Pod IP changes.

useCases.title: Use cluster DNS
useCases.scenario: An application needs to discover another Service by name.

useCases.title: Expose with NodePort or LoadBalancer
useCases.scenario: A Service must be reachable from outside the cluster.

interview.question: What problem does a Kubernetes Service solve?
interview.answer: A Service is a stable network endpoint for a logical group of Pods. Its selector finds matching Pods, and traffic is load-balanced to one of them.
interview.followUp: How does Kubernetes track the selected Pods? The selector is evaluated continuously, and matching Pod addresses are written to an EndpointSlice; removed or new Pods update that slice.

interview.question: What is the difference between port and targetPort?
interview.answer: The Service port is the port clients use to reach the Service. The targetPort is the port that accepts traffic on each selected Pod.
interview.followUp: Can targetPort be a name? Yes. The example documentation says it can be a name such as www or a number such as 80.

interview.question: How can a Pod find a Service?
interview.answer: A ClusterIP Service is reachable inside the cluster through its stable cluster IP. Kubernetes DNS can also resolve the Service name, such as my-nginx, to that IP.
interview.followUp: What if the DNS add-on is not running? Service-name lookups will not work until the cluster DNS add-on, such as CoreDNS, is enabled.

keyPoints: Each Pod gets its own cluster-private IP, so Pods can communicate without manually linking them or mapping container ports to node ports.
A Service receives a stable cluster IP that remains unchanged for the Service lifetime.
Clients use the Service instead of individual Pod IPs, and Kubernetes distributes requests across matching Pods.
Kubernetes keeps EndpointSlices aligned with the Service selector, adding matching Pods and removing dead Pods.
A selector chooses the Pods behind a Service, while the port settings define how TCP traffic reaches them.
Cluster DNS lets Pods use a Service name instead of its cluster IP.
gotchas: Service environment variables are added only when a Pod starts, so create the Service before creating the Pods if applications need those variables.
Creating replicas before the Service can also miss the scheduler-level spreading described by the tutorial.
Set enableServiceLinks to false when automatic Service environment variables are unwanted.

Observability.summary: Kubernetes observability collects and analyzes metrics, logs, and traces. These signals help show the health, performance, and internal state of a cluster.
Observability.explanation: Kubernetes observability combines metrics, logs, and traces to show cluster health and behavior. Components emit signals, pipelines collect them, storage systems keep them, and dashboards, alerts, or automation use the results.

example.title: A simple metrics pipeline
example.code:
# Scrape component metrics and store them in a time-series database.
# Example Prometheus configuration fragment:
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: kubernetes-components
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - kube-apiserver:6443
          - kube-scheduler:10259
example.explanation: This shows the general shape of a metrics scrape configuration. The exact targets and access settings depend on the cluster.

useCases.title: Monitor cluster health
useCases.scenario: Use metrics to build dashboards and alerts for component behavior and resource use.

useCases.title: Investigate events
useCases.scenario: Use logs from applications, control plane components, and audit records in one central store.

useCases.title: Debug distributed requests
useCases.scenario: Follow a request across components to find latency, bottlenecks, or unexpected interactions.

interview.question: What are the three pillars of Kubernetes observability?
interview.answer: The three pillars are metrics, logs, and traces. Metrics describe measured values over time, logs record events, and traces connect work across components and applications.
interview.followUp: How would you connect them during an incident? Use shared time ranges and useful identifiers to correlate an alert, related log entries, and the trace for the affected request.

interview.question: How does a common Kubernetes metrics pipeline work?
interview.answer: Kubernetes components expose metrics in Prometheus format through metrics endpoints. A usual pipeline scrapes those endpoints and stores the samples in time-series storage for dashboards and alerts.
interview.followUp: What extra endpoint does the kubelet provide for resource metrics? It exposes /metrics/resource, alongside its other kubelet metrics endpoints.

interview.question: How are traces collected and stored?
interview.answer: Tracing follows requests across Kubernetes components and applications. OTLP exporters send spans directly or through an OpenTelemetry Collector, which can process them before forwarding them to a tracing backend.
interview.followUp: Why place a collector between exporters and storage? It can apply processing such as sampling or redaction and then export the result to the backend.

keyPoints: Observability uses three signal types: metrics, logs, and traces.
Combining the signals gives a broader view of the control plane, add-ons, and applications.
Several Kubernetes components publish metrics in Prometheus format through /metrics.
Add-ons can add object-state information to the metrics produced by core components.
A metrics pipeline regularly reads endpoints and saves the values in time-series storage.
Traces show request movement and help connect timing and relationships between operations.
gotchas: Do not assume that the kubelet has only one metrics endpoint. Different endpoints provide different kinds of data.
Tools listed in the observability documentation are not maintained or supported by the Kubernetes project.
A tracing pipeline may change spans before storage, such as by sampling or redacting them.

OpenTelemetry.summary: Kubernetes system tracing records operation timing and relationships as spans. Components export these spans with OTLP over gRPC to an OpenTelemetry Collector or directly to a tracing backend.
OpenTelemetry.explanation: Kubernetes components create spans that describe operation timing and relationships. They export the spans with OTLP over gRPC, either directly to a tracing backend or through an OpenTelemetry Collector. The collector can process and forward the data to storage and analysis tools.

parameters.name: tracing.endpoint
parameters.description: OTLP gRPC destination for exported spans.

parameters.name: tracing.samplingRatePerMillion
parameters.description: Number of spans sampled per million when there is no parent sampling decision.

apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
tracing:
  endpoint: localhost:4317

interview.question: What problem does Kubernetes system tracing solve?
interview.answer: Kubernetes component tracing records operation timing and relationships. Components export spans using OTLP over gRPC, either to an OpenTelemetry Collector or directly to a tracing backend.

interview.question: How do you enable tracing for the kubelet?
interview.answer: Configure tracing for the component and set an OTLP endpoint. For the kubelet, the configuration uses a tracing block with endpoint and samplingRatePerMillion fields.
interview.followUp: How can you send every span? Set samplingRatePerMillion to 1000000.

interview.question: How are kubelet and container-runtime traces linked?
interview.answer: The kubelet propagates trace context through gRPC requests. Instrumented container runtimes can then connect their spans to kubelet spans, creating parent-child relationships for node troubleshooting.

keyPoints: System traces show how long operations take and how operations relate to one another.
Kubernetes uses OTLP over gRPC to send component spans.
The API server traces incoming HTTP requests and selected outgoing requests.
The kubelet passes trace context through gRPC calls so other components can join the same trace.

An OpenTelemetry Collector can receive spans, process them, and send them to a tracing backend.

kind: Deployment
metadata:

spec:

---
apiVersion: example.com/v1
kind: SampleDB
metadata:
  name: example-database
spec:
  version: "1.0"
example.explanation: The Deployment runs the operator controller. The SampleDB custom resource declares the database that the controller manages.

interview.question: What is a Kubernetes Operator?
interview.answer: An Operator is a Kubernetes API client that acts as a controller for a custom resource. It watches the resource and reconciles the cluster toward the state declared by the user.
interview.followUp: Why use a custom resource? It adds an application-specific API object without changing Kubernetes core code.

interview.question: How is an Operator deployed?
interview.answer: Deploy the CustomResourceDefinition and its controller. The controller commonly runs as a containerized application in a Deployment outside the control plane.
interview.followUp: What must a user do after installation? Create, update, or delete the custom resource managed by the Operator.

interview.question: What work can an Operator automate?
interview.answer: When a SampleDB resource is created, the controller can create storage, a StatefulSet, and an initialization Job. It can also manage backups, upgrades, and cleanup when the resource is deleted.
interview.followUp: How does the controller know what to change? It queries the API server and runs reconciliation until actual state matches the resource configuration.

Its controller repeatedly reconciles desired state with the current state.
Operators add behavior through the Kubernetes API instead of changing Kubernetes source code.
The controller watches the custom resource and manages related Kubernetes objects.
Installation normally adds the CRD and the associated controller to the cluster.
Users operate the application by creating, changing, or removing its custom resource.
gotchas: The controller is usually deployed separately from the Kubernetes control plane, often as a Deployment.
If no existing operator provides the needed behavior, you can build one using any language or runtime that can call the Kubernetes API.

interview.answer: kubectl is the main command-line tool for running commands and managing Kubernetes clusters. It communicates with the Kubernetes API.

PersistentVolume.summary: A PersistentVolume (PV) is cluster storage created by an administrator or through dynamic provisioning. A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) requests storage, and Kubernetes binds a matching PVC to one PV.
PersistentVolume.explanation: A PersistentVolume (PV) is cluster storage created by an administrator or through dynamic provisioning. A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) requests storage, and Kubernetes binds a matching PVC to one PV. A Pod uses the PVC, not the PV directly.

parameters.name: spec.resources.requests.storage
parameters.description: The storage requested by the claim, such as 3Gi.

parameters.name: spec.accessModes
parameters.description: The requested access mode, such as ReadWriteOnce.

parameters.name: spec.storageClassName
parameters.description: The StorageClass associated with the PV or requested by the PVC.

parameters.name: spec.persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy
parameters.description: The reclaim action after the claim is released.

example.title: Create a PersistentVolume
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: task-pv-volume
spec:
  storageClassName: manual
  capacity:
    storage: 10Gi
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data
example.explanation: This creates a 10 GiB PV using a host directory. A matching PVC can later bind to it.

interview.question: What are PVs and PVCs, and how are they related?
interview.answer: A PV is cluster storage with a lifecycle independent of a Pod. A PVC is a user's storage request. Kubernetes binds a matching PVC to one PV, and a Pod mounts the PVC.
interview.followUp: What happens when no PV matches? The claim stays unbound until a matching PV becomes available, or dynamic provisioning creates one through a requested StorageClass.

interview.question: Compare static and dynamic provisioning.
interview.answer: Static provisioning means an administrator creates PVs first. Dynamic provisioning creates a volume when no existing PV matches a PVC, using the requested StorageClass.
interview.followUp: How can a PVC disable dynamic provisioning? Set its storageClassName to an empty string explicitly.

interview.question: What does a PV reclaim policy do?
interview.answer: The reclaim policy controls what happens after a PV is released. Retain keeps the storage for manual recovery, Delete removes the PV and supported external storage, and Recycle is deprecated.
interview.followUp: What is inherited by dynamically provisioned PVs? They inherit the StorageClass reclaim policy, whose default is Delete.

keyPoints: A PV is a cluster resource, similar to a node.
A PV can outlive the Pod that uses it.
A PVC can request storage size and access modes such as ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany, or ReadWriteOncePod.
One PVC binds to one PV.
The reclaim policy decides how released storage is handled.
PV node affinity limits which nodes can use the volume and affects Pod scheduling.
gotchas: Use hostPath only for single-node development or testing. It is not supported for reliable multi-node storage.
Do not choose Recycle for new designs. Prefer dynamic provisioning or another supported reclaim policy.
PVC expansion resizes the existing backing volume. It does not create another PV.
Increase the PVC size to request expansion. Do not edit PV capacity directly.

PersistentVolumeClaim.summary: A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a user's request for persistent storage. Kubernetes matches it with a suitable PersistentVolume (PV), then a Pod can mount the claim without naming the storage implementation directly.
PersistentVolumeClaim.explanation: A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a user's request for persistent storage. Kubernetes matches it with a suitable PersistentVolume (PV), then a Pod can mount the claim without naming the storage implementation directly.
PersistentVolumeClaim.syntax:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: <claim-name>
spec:
  accessModes: [<mode>]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: <size>

parameters.name: spec.accessModes
parameters.description: Requested volume access modes, such as ReadWriteOnce or ReadOnlyMany.

parameters.name: spec.resources
parameters.description: Minimum storage capacity requested by the claim.

parameters.name: spec.storageClassName
parameters.description: StorageClass required by the claim.

parameters.name: spec.volumeName
parameters.description: Reference to the PersistentVolume that backs the claim.

parameters.name: spec.volumeMode
parameters.description: Requested volume type: Filesystem or Block.

parameters.name: spec.selector
parameters.description: Optional label query used to select candidate volumes.

PersistentVolumeClaim.returns: A PersistentVolumeClaim object with desired settings in spec and current information in status. Its phase can be Pending, Bound, or Lost.

example.title: Claim storage and mount it in a Pod
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: data
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 3Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nginx
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: data
example.explanation: The claim requests storage. The Pod then uses that claim as a volume.

interview.question: What are a PV and a PVC, and how do they work together?
interview.answer: A PVC is a user's storage request. A PV is cluster storage supplied by an administrator or by dynamic provisioning. Kubernetes binds a suitable PV to the PVC, and a Pod mounts the PVC.
interview.followUp: What happens if no matching PV exists? The PVC stays unbound until a matching volume becomes available, unless dynamic provisioning creates one.

interview.question: How does a Pod use a PVC?
interview.answer: A Pod lists a PVC in its volumes block with persistentVolumeClaim.claimName. The Pod does not need to specify the underlying PV; the claim represents the storage from the Pod's perspective.
interview.followUp: Can one PV be mounted at different paths in one container? Yes. The tutorial shows two volumeMounts using the same volume with different subPath values.

interview.question: Which fields affect PVC binding?
interview.answer: A PVC requests storage size, access modes, and optionally a StorageClass. The control plane uses these requirements to find or provision a suitable PV and then binds the two resources.
interview.followUp: How can a PVC target one particular PV? Set volumeName on the PVC and reserve the PV with a matching claimRef when other claims must be prevented from using it.

keyPoints: A PVC describes the storage a user wants, rather than how the storage is implemented.
Pods use node capacity, while PVCs request capacity from PV resources.
A PVC can remain Pending until Kubernetes finds or provisions a compatible PV.
A Pod mounts storage by referring to the PVC in its volumes section.
A PVC can request a filesystem volume or a raw block device. Filesystem is the default.
PVC expansion is stable and enabled by default in Kubernetes v1.24 and later, subject to the StorageClass and driver requirements.
gotchas: A PVC can grow only when its StorageClass allows expansion. Kubernetes resizes the existing volume; it does not create a replacement.
A failed expansion can be retried with a smaller request, but the request must remain above the current capacity.
A bound PVC and PV form an exclusive one-to-one relationship.

Pod.explanation: A Pod is a Kubernetes object that runs one or more containers together on one Node. kind: Pod
metadata:

spec:

interview.question: What is a Pod?
interview.answer: A Pod is the smallest deployable Kubernetes unit. It contains one or more containers that are co-located, co-scheduled, and run in a shared context. Containers in the same Pod share networking and may share volumes.
interview.followUp: Why not put every container in one Pod? Containers should share a Pod only when they are tightly coupled and need shared resources. Independent components should use separate Pods.

interview.question: How do containers in one Pod share networking?
interview.answer: A Pod gets one IP address for each address family, and its containers share the network namespace. Containers in the same Pod can reach one another through localhost, but they must coordinate port use.
interview.followUp: How do containers in different Pods communicate? The page states the same-Pod localhost behavior, but a practical design normally uses Kubernetes networking and a Service for stable access.

interview.question: Why are Pods usually managed by workload resources?
interview.answer: Usually, create a Deployment, Job, or StatefulSet instead of creating a Pod directly. The workload controller creates and manages Pods, including replication, rollout, and replacement after failures.
interview.followUp: What happens after a Node fails? A controller detects that the Pod is no longer working, creates a replacement, and the scheduler places it on a healthy Node.

keyPoints: All containers in a Pod share its network namespace, IP address, and ports.
Containers in the same Pod can communicate through localhost.
Volumes let containers in one Pod share data and can preserve data when a container restarts.
Prefer workload resources such as Deployments, Jobs, or StatefulSets for creating Pods.
The scheduler places each Pod on a Node, where the kubelet manages its containers.
gotchas: Do not treat a Pod as a permanent machine. A Pod can end because it finishes, is deleted, is evicted, or its Node fails.
A running Pod cannot gain or lose regular containers. Use a workload resource to create replacement Pods when the container layout changes.
Multiple containers in one Pod are for tightly coupled parts that share resources. Do not use them simply to create replicas.
The Pod OS must match the Node OS. In a mixed-OS cluster, also use an OS nodeSelector because the scheduler does not use .spec.os.name to choose a Node.

Prometheus.summary: Kubernetes observability collects metrics, logs, and traces to show cluster health and behavior. Metrics endpoints can be scraped and stored for dashboards, alerts, and automation.
Prometheus.explanation: Kubernetes observability collects metrics, logs, and traces from cluster components and add-ons. Metrics endpoints are commonly scraped by Prometheus, stored as time series, and used for dashboards, alerts, or automated actions.

example.title: Deploy an exporter for Prometheus
example.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-exporter
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: my-exporter
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: my-exporter
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: exporter
        image: example.com/my-exporter:v1.0.0
        ports:
        - name: metrics
          containerPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-exporter
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: my-exporter
  ports:
  - name: metrics
    port: 8080
    targetPort: metrics
example.explanation: This runs the exporter and gives Prometheus a stable Service address. The exporter must serve metrics at /metrics on the named metrics port.

interview.answer: Kubernetes observability uses metrics, logs, and traces. Collecting and correlating all three gives information about cluster state, performance, and health.
